What the line includes and how it is used

Specifications show how the line is positioned:

  • Ports tolerate up to 2,000 punctures with a 22G Huber needle. Power versions are rated to 5 ml/s for CT contrast.
  • HealthPICC kits bundle accessories from other makers: a MicroCLAVE connector from ICU Medical and a Grip-Lok securement device from TIDI.
  • The Secureport PLP port was listed among purchased stock-in-trade in the 2024 placement document. At least part of the port range is therefore traded rather than made at the reporting level.

The unit economics differ from infusion. A port patient generates a Huber needle for every chemotherapy cycle and maintenance items for the life of the port, so the installed base of ports drives recurring volume.

Plan1Health: the Italian base

History.

  • The company: Plan1Health, of Amaro in north-east Italy, dates from 1995 on Polymed's slides. The 2024 placement document says it was incorporated in 1990.
  • The purchase: Poly Medicure B.V. paid EUR 3,468,600 and EUR 761,400 on 18 June 2018 and 6 March 2019, booking goodwill of €3.83mn. That is why Polymed's documents date the deal both FY18 (Rs. 342mn, placement document) and 2019 (enterprise value ~€4.2mn, company slide).
  • Scale: it had 31 employees in CY25.

What it makes. Management describes Plan1Health as a maker of long-term infusion devices, oncology products and "an innovative pain-control device", and as "a Class III implantables specialist and sole approved supplier to one of the largest OEMs for Class III implants" (Section A4.10).

  • Europe: it sells through 20+ distributors, with its whole portfolio of four categories approved.
  • US: its only clearance is the Painfusor catheter (K111031, 2011), which the company describes as an approval held for an OEM.
  • Italy: it gives the group its only direct sales operation in Europe.

Growth and margins. Plan1Health's revenue fell 5% in the COVID year, then grew 30% (FY22), ~50% (9MFY24) and 40%+ (FY24). Management said it was still growing 30-35% in Feb-2026.

The margin record is less clear, as Exhibit 25 shows. Management has described the EBITDA margin as "almost 16-17%" for FY24 and "around close to 16%-17%" in Nov-2025, yet its own acquisition slide shows 10.9% for CY24 and 13.4% for CY25. The statutory Italian accounts give an EBIT margin of 10.2% in CY25 (our calculation) and net profit of €681k. We use the slide figures, which fit the statutory EBIT, and treat the higher figures as management rounding or a different definition.

The company's own slides also disagree on the margin gain since the acquisition: 970bps (1QFY27 deck), ~670bps (Sep-2026 AGM deck) and ~600bps (4QFY26 deck). The 1QFY27 deck also claims 3.2x revenue and 11.8x EBITDA growth since 2020.

Links with the parent.

  • Trade: Polymed sold goods worth Rs. 147mn to Plan1Health in FY26.
  • Management: Plan1Health's founder and chief executive, Alessandro Balboni, also runs Polymed's EMEA business and sits on its board as a non-independent director. He was paid management fees of Rs. 29mn in FY26 (Section A9).
  • The "P1H playbook": management presents Plan1Health as the model for PendraCare and Citieffe: faster launches, manufacturing moved to India to cut cost, direct sales, wider distribution and joint R&D.

Oncology in Vision 2030 and in India

Management lists oncology among the five focus areas for the next five years, with orthopaedics, cardiology, neonatology and renal care, because these carry higher gross margins than infusion.

The Indian plan has four strands:

  • Local manufacture. Oncology products are sold in India through the critical-care team. Products "currently made in Italy" are to be moved to India, where management says demand is 80-90% imported.
  • Higher-class devices. Chemoports, a Class III implantable, have been launched in India. Management frames this as a shift from short-term devices to "longer term use devices" in Class III, with competition mostly from multinationals and "a couple of good Indian companies also like Meril".
  • Public cancer care. The government is setting up standalone specialty oncology (day-care) centres: 200 in FY26 and 700 over three years, on management's account.
  • New products. Recent launches include neonatal PICCs of 1Fr & 2Fr ("one of the first" made in India), an antimicrobial CVC, tear-away introducers, midlines, PICC-ports and a safety Huber needle.

Market and competition

Commercial research firms (vendor estimates, used as indications only) put these global markets at:

  • implantable ports: $1.4bn in 2025;
  • PICCs: $1.43bn in 2026;
  • central venous catheters: $3.07bn in 2026;
  • catheter introducer sheaths: $1.93bn by 2030.

Their company lists put B. Braun, BD, Cook Medical, AngioDynamics, Smiths Medical and Teleflex in ports and PICCs. Poly Medicure is listed among PICC and CVC suppliers.

The large competitors are:

  • BD: ports sit within its Peripheral Intervention unit ($2.0bn revenue in FY25), and PICCs and midlines within Medication Delivery Solutions.
  • Teleflex: its Arrow-branded vascular catheters generated $917.7mn in CY25.
  • ICU Medical: it sells Port-A-Cath ports, PowerWand midlines and Deltec Gripper non-coring needles within a consumables business of $1.1bn.

In India, management names multinationals and Meril as the competitors in oncology implants.

We see Plan1Health's advantage as regulatory, not scale. It holds MDR approval for its whole portfolio and supplies a Class III OEM, and management says each country registration takes two to three years. Polymed's contribution is lower-cost manufacturing and a distribution network in 125+ countries.

Regulation specific to the line

  • Class III. Ports are Class III implants, the highest risk class in Europe. Management says Class III devices take "very much, much longer to register", often two to three years including clinical trials.
  • Italian payback. A 2015 Italian law requires device suppliers to pay the government when regional device spending exceeds annual ceilings; the Constitutional Court upheld it in Jul-2024. BD booked a $62mn accrual for it in FY24 and settled at 25% of invoiced amounts. Italian public spending on medical devices and services is about €10bn a year, according to the industry association Confindustria Dispositivi Medici. Plan1Health sells directly to Italian hospitals, so it is presumably exposed, but its exposure is [not disclosed].
  • EU procurement. Since Jun-2025 the EU has excluded Chinese bidders from public medical-device tenders worth €5mn or more (Section A4.1). For a direct seller to Italian hospitals such as Plan1Health, that removes low-cost rivals from the larger tenders (our view).
  • US. Beyond Painfusor, Plan1Health has FDA submissions "under evaluation".

Growth and margin drivers, ranked

  1. India import substitution in ports and PICCs (management target; our view: largest long-run lever). The drivers are chemotherapy volumes, the day-care cancer centres and hospitals preferring local suppliers as insurance spreads. Timing depends on moving Plan1Health products to Indian manufacture and approval.
  2. Plan1Health's European growth (management: 30-35% a year). The levers are the new MDR filings for oncology, neonatal and pain products and cross-selling Polymed products through Plan1Health in Italy.
  3. Recurring consumables per port (our view). Huber needles and maintenance items follow the installed base of ports.
  4. Margin: scale and Indian manufacturing (company target). The company-reported EBITDA margin rose from 3.7% to 13.4% as revenue tripled. Management expects moving labour-heavy processes to India to add more.
  5. Risk: Italian payback and tender pricing (our view). This offsets part of the gain.

What to watch

Open questions for management (also in the question bank):

  • oncology and vascular-access revenue at group level;
  • which Plan1Health products are made in Italy, bought in, or being moved to India;
  • the definition behind management's higher EBITDA margin figures for Plan1Health;
  • any Italian payback accruals;
  • the identity and terms of the Class III OEM customer.

A4.3 Renal care

Renal is Polymed's second line and, until FY26, its fastest-growing one: a full haemodialysis consumables basket plus an Indian-made machine, sold into a market where the only other local dialyser plant is an export unit and where pricing is set by Chinese imports that enter duty-free through South-East Asia. The line's next leg depends on two things outside Polymed's control, a trade-remedy ruling and public dialysis tenders, and on one inside it, turning a small installed base of machines into consumables pull-through.

Renal care at a glance

Revenue FY26
Rs. 1.9bn (+24.5% yoy), 10% of consolidated revenue
Revenue 1QFY27
Rs. 432mn (-3.8% yoy), 8% of consolidated revenue
Long-run growth
Company FY20-FY26 CAGR 39%; FY26 revenue 19x FY18's (our calculation)
Machines
450 units placed in FY26; installed base ~1,100 units (Aug-2026)
Share (management)
10% of the Indian market (Feb-2026); target 15-17% in two to three years
Policy
Anti-dumping case on Chinese and Malaysian dialysers opened on Polymed's petition (25 Jun 2026); PLI-approved, no incentive received
What is disclosed
Annual and quarterly renal revenue, machines placed; no split between dialysers, bloodlines, needles and machines; no segment margin

What it is and how it is used: one session, one set of consumables

In haemodialysis the patient's blood is pumped from an arteriovenous fistula in the arm through a dialyser, where toxins and excess water cross a hollow-fibre membrane into dialysate that the machine prepares from purified water and concentrates, and back into the vein. Each three-to-five-hour session uses:

  • a pair of AV fistula needles (arterial and venous), always single use, the cleanest per-session consumable;
  • one bloodline set and usually two transducer protectors;
  • one dialyser, which Indian centres commonly reprocess and reuse for the same patient;
  • acid and bicarbonate concentrates, which Polymed's catalogues do not list.

Temporary access (acute kidney injury, or while a fistula matures) uses a haemodialysis catheter kit, and acute bedside peritoneal dialysis uses a stiff PD catheter set. A machine is a one-off sale that then runs three to four treatments a day, which is why management describes machines as only ~10% of renal revenue and consumables as the rest.

The unit of demand is the session. Frost & Sullivan (Nov-2025, via the NephroPlus prospectus) puts India's in-clinic treatments at 33.9mn in 2024, rising to 66.1mn by 2029 (14.3% CAGR, our calculation), for 0.28mn patients. In-clinic haemodialysis is more than 98% of all dialysis in India, and only 50% of patients are dialysed three times a week, against the two to three sessions a week that is typical. At a single-use pair per session, 2024 treatments imply ~67.8mn units fistula needles a year (our calculation).

Dialyser demand is sessions divided by reuse, and reuse is the swing factor.

  • The MD described reuse ranging from single use to ten times in Mumbai centres, 7 to 8 on average and a single-use share of only 20-25% (both Aug-2023). The industry benchmark is a Fresenius dialyser reused seven times.
  • By Oct-2024 he put single use at 30-35% of the market (from 10% when Polymed entered), heading to 50% in two to three years. That would raise dialyser consumption without a single extra session.
  • Against that, the largest chain, NephroPlus, reprocesses dialysers for the same patient with its own patented Renova system, and CDSCO says it has received no complaints about reuse of single-use devices in five years.
  • Management sized Indian consumption at 8mn units to 12mn units dialysers a year (Feb-2023).

Polymed's portfolio and position

Polymed makes every item in the session except concentrates, under its own brands:

  • Dial-Ezee haemodialysis machine: touchscreen, bicarbonate dialysis with ultrafiltration and sodium profiling, inbuilt SLED, variable dialysate flow of 100 to 800 ml/min, single or dual blood pump, and an optional Polytox endotoxin filter that fits only Dial-Ezee.
  • Haem-O-Flux dialyser: PES membrane, mid and high flux, three surface-area variants, shelf life 36 months.
  • Haem-O-Line bloodlines (pre- and post-pump) with a shelf life of 60 months, and transducer protectors.
  • AV fistula needles in 15G, 16G and 17G, plus the Poly Protekt safety fistula needle.
  • Haemocent and Haemocent Pro double- and triple-lumen haemodialysis catheter kits, also sold as components.
  • Peritoneal dialysis set and Y-shaped PD transfusion set, for acute rather than home PD.

How the line was built.

  • Fistula needles, bloodlines, HD catheters and PD sets were already in the FY16 range. The company dates its renal entry to 2018 and launched its dialyser in FY19; it describes itself as the first Indian company to make dialysers indigenously, a claim CRISIL repeats.
  • The machine came in two steps. Polymed first resold an imported machine from Jul-2020, and haemodialysis machines appear among traded goods in the placement document; the whole traded line, which also held blood-collection tubes, was only Rs. 88mn in FY22.
  • Its own machine came out of clinical trials with assembly starting in Aug-2022. Local content rose from ~35% to more than 50%+ by Feb-2024, with circuit boards moved from Taiwanese and Korean suppliers to Bangalore, and the MD says it was the first dialysis machine to receive BIS certification.
  • In the pipeline: an HDF (haemodiafiltration) machine made in India, targeted for mid-to-end 2026, 7-8 further renal products, and a pain-reducing needle technology.

Capacity and service.

  • Renal capacity was tripled over FY22 (three times per the plan), with dialysis capacity at the IMT Faridabad plant "almost double" by May-2022. A further "tripling" was planned from FY25, after Polymed said in Oct-2024 that it was "short of products right now". Capacity was to "almost double" again by end-FY26.
  • The PLI project at Faridabad is shown as commissioned, with Rs. 556mn invested against Rs. 720mn committed. A separate government grant of Rs. 100mn supports a Rs. 1.0bn project for polymer tubing components, including bloodline and dialysis accessories.
  • Service is the differentiator management stresses: 30+ engineers, each able to cover 20-30 machines, and a three-year warranty followed by service contracts. There is "no significant service revenue".

Revenue: nineteen-fold in eight years, then a stall

Renal revenue rose from Rs. 99mn in FY18 to Rs. 1.9bn in FY26, 19x on our calculation, lifting its share of the product table from 1.9% to 10% of consolidated revenue. Growth was uneven:

  • FY23-FY24: 27% and 25% on the placement-document figures (our calculation), against management's descriptions of around 40% for FY23 and 21-22% for FY24.
  • FY25: 60% (our calculation; the company's standalone figure is 60.1%). Management credited mandatory licensing of devices from Oct-2023, which it said ended unregulated parallel imports, and a rise in dialysis reimbursement from Rs. 1,200 to Rs. 1,800 per session that drew more standalone centres.
  • FY26: +24.5% as reported, which the MD described on the call as growth of "close to around 20%". Management gave three reasons:
    1. distributor inventory realignment around the Sep-2025 GST cut (2QFY26);
    2. pressure from Chinese suppliers (3QFY26);
    3. government contracts delayed by budgeting.
  • 1QFY27: revenue fell 3.8% to Rs. 432mn because Polymed "made a conscious choice to raise prices to push the raw material price increase rather than defend volume at any cost".

The quarterly run-rate shows where the growth went. Revenue held between Rs. 442mn and Rs. 449mn in each of the first three quarters of FY26, jumped 25.4% qoq in 4QFY26 (our calculation) and fell back to Rs. 432mn in 1QFY27. The four FY26 quarters as last reported sum to Rs. 1.9bn (our calculation), slightly above the annual Rs. 1.9bn, because the 1QFY27 deck restated 1QFY26 from Rs. 435mn to Rs. 449mn.

The guidance record. Renal has been the least reliable line in Polymed's guidance (Section A3). Revenue targets were cut in four of the five years from FY23 to FY27, and machine targets were cut in every year from FY24 to FY26. The one beat, FY25, followed the start of device licensing.

Machines and the installed base: razor and blades, but not locked in

The machine is the entry ticket to a dialysis unit's consumables, but Polymed's model differs from the MNCs'.

  • The MNC model. Fresenius and Nipro "place machines in the hospital" and then supply consumables under contracts of 5 to 7 years, which their balance sheets allow.
  • Polymed's model. Polymed sells the machine outright, for ~Rs. 0.5-0.6mn per unit (May-2023), priced 5-7% below MNC machines, and relies on service and local content to win the consumables.

Polymed's ~1,100 units machines are only 2.8% of India's ~40,000 (our calculation on F&S's installed base). Management's ~10% share claim therefore implies that most of its dialysers, bloodlines and needles go into other brands' machines. Dialysers and needles are not machine-specific, so we read the installed base as a door-opener rather than a lock-in.

The scale gap is wide. Fresenius and Nipro have "installations of over 40,000-50,000 machines" in India, and the MD has put Fresenius alone at 70%-80% of India's installed base. NephroPlus alone ran 5,562 machines in Sep-2025, having added 1,900 since Mar-2023 (our calculation), more than Polymed's entire installed base.

The FY26 shortfall against the machine target came from tenders. Management said that "certain government contracts are delayed", that it had bid for more than 600 machines, and that its current visibility for FY26 was 450 units machines ("it can be 470 also"), with the rest likely to slip into FY27 "because of budgeting issues".

Market: India's dialysis is growing fast, but through public programmes and price-driven chains

Demand and capacity (Frost & Sullivan via the NephroPlus prospectus; vendor-commissioned, Nov-2025):

  • India had 4.2mn diagnosed ESRD patients in 2024, but only 0.28mn were on dialysis. That is forecast to reach 0.52mn by 2029, a 12.7% CAGR.
  • It has ~5,000 dialysis clinics, more than 80% of them private, and ~40,000 machines against a stated need of more than 105,000.
  • The organized chains hold ~20% of a services market of $818.0mn (2024) that F&S expects to reach $2.0bn by 2029.

The MD's own sizing was ~~Rs. 10.0bn in May-2021, 95% of it imported. By May-2023 he put the market at Rs. 10-11bn, of which consumables were Rs. 8-9bn and machines Rs. 2.0-2.5bn, on 3,000-4,000 machine sales a year. He put industry growth at ~25% in May-2025.

Public money sets the price. Management estimates that 70-80% of patients are treated in government-funded centres, and the programmes pay per session:

  • PMNDP. The Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme, launched in 2016, runs 1,925 centres with 13,824 haemodialysis machines in 751 districts (dashboard, Sep-2026). Those machines are 35% of F&S's national installed base (our calculation; different dates). Annual sessions rose from 2.5mn to 7.0mn in five years.
  • PPP model. Where PMNDP runs as a PPP (in 14 states and UTs), the private partner supplies the machines, water plant, dialysers and consumables. Contracts run 5 years (extendable), at a bid price that escalates 3% a year.
  • PM-JAY. The insurer pays Rs. 1,500 per haemodialysis session in tier-3 cities and Rs. 1,800 in tier-1 and tier-2 (HBP 2022); F&S puts the average at Rs. 1,650.

Polymed's consumables are therefore bought mainly by PPP operators and chains that bid for low per-session rates.

Private chains are consolidating the buying. NephroPlus is the largest. It served 29,281 patients in FY25, ~10% of India's dialysis patients, from 468 clinics (176 of them under PPP). DCDC runs more than 200 PPP clinics; Apex Kidney Care, Apollo Dialysis, RAHI Care, VitusCare and 7Med follow.

The chains buy centrally and are integrating backwards:

  • NephroPlus sources the dialysers, bloodlines and fistula needles for its Indian clinics within India.
  • It owns proprietary bloodline moulds and has contract manufacturers assemble the sets.
  • It reprocesses dialysers.

Its whole materials bill, across India, the Philippines and Uzbekistan, was Rs. 1.9bn in FY25, about the size of Polymed's renal revenue.

Polymed counts NephroPlus and DCDC among its customers, which makes the chains both the growth channel and the main source of price pressure.

Global context. Fresenius Medical Care's 20-F (CY25) gives the frame:

  • 4.5mn patients worldwide, growing 4-5% a year, 89% of them on in-centre haemodialysis;
  • a global dialysis market of €81-85bn, of which €16bn is products;
  • ~450mn units dialysers sold a year, 38% of them made by Fresenius;
  • 110,000 units haemodialysis machines installed in 2025, ~50% of them by Fresenius.

Vendor estimates put the global dialyser market at $4.0bn (IMARC, 2025) and haemodialysis catheters at $1.11bn (360iResearch, 2026).

Competition: MNCs above, Chinese imports below, and no Indian peer

Polymed positions itself between the two tiers on price. Its machines sell 5-7% below MNC machines, and Chinese consumables were ~15% cheaper than Polymed's in May-2023. Against both, it offers local service and training ("Chinese don't offer any service"), local content for public buyers, and a full consumables basket including a safety fistula needle.

Under public procurement rules, a Class-I local supplier needs at least 50% local content. The machine's ~50% local content is at that threshold. A Department of Pharmaceuticals order of Oct-2024 that deems PLI makers Class-II suppliers lists Nipro for dialysers but not Polymed, although a maker can still qualify as Class-I on its own content.

Regulation and policy: duty inversion, a trade-remedy case and a PLI that has not paid

Tariffs and the inverted duty structure.

  • Dialysers were duty-free until the Feb-2022 Budget imposed 7.5%. Management says Chinese makers then shifted to bases in ASEAN countries and relabelled product there to enter India at zero duty under the ASEAN FTA.
  • In May-2026 the MD put Chinese imports at "0% duty, only 5% GST" on the finished product. Polymed, by contrast, pays 2.5% customs duty on imported raw materials and 18% GST on inputs.
  • The FY26 annual report names renal as the segment hit by this duty inversion and by "dumping from China".

Imports under the dialysis tariff line (HS 90189031, which also covers machines) show the route shifting:

  • China. Declared quantities fell 39% in FY26 to 10.6mn units (our calculation).
  • Malaysia and Hong Kong. Malaysia rose 38% to 6.1mn units, and Hong Kong jumped to 2.5mn units.
  • By value. China's share of the line fell from 35% in FY23 to 21% in FY26, while Malaysia and Hong Kong reached 18%. The line's total value grew 37% over FY23-FY26 (our calculation).

We read this as consistent with management's account of Chinese product being rerouted, not as proof of it.

The anti-dumping case. The Directorate General of Trade Remedies opened Case AD (OI) (17/2026) on 25 Jun 2026 on Polymed's application.

  • Scope. The case covers disposable dialysers from China and Malaysia, with product types defined by surface area and flux; housing material was added in Aug-2026. Named Fresenius brands are excluded, which we read as targeting the low-priced product rather than the premium MNC lines.
  • Periods. The period of investigation is CY25, and the injury period runs from FY23.
  • Standing. Polymed is "the major domestic producer". The only other producer, Nipro Medical India, is a 100% export-oriented unit.
  • The injury claim, as summarized by DGTR. Subject imports rose "significantly in absolute terms", with price undercutting and depression, and the domestic industry "has incurred financial losses, cash losses and negative return on capital employed during the period of investigation". This is the first disclosure of the economics of Polymed's dialyser business.
  • Status. 11 parties registered, including five Chinese producers, a Malaysian producer and two importers. Questionnaire responses were due by 9 Sep 2026, and no preliminary findings had been published by 24 Sep 2026.
  • Management's view. Management has claimed an injury margin of 20% and expects "something will happen between now and end of the year". It has also raised the issue with the Health Minister.

PLI: approved, invested, unpaid.

  • Approval. Polymed is a Category A applicant under Target Segment 3 (anaesthetics, cardio-respiratory and renal-care devices) for seven products made at Faridabad: dialyser, machine, PD kit, fistula needle, bloodline, haemodialysis catheter and transducer protector.
  • Terms. The scheme pays 5% on incremental sales over FY20. A Category A applicant must show incremental sales of at least Rs. 600mn in FY23, rising to Rs. 2.3bn in FY26 and Rs. 2.8bn in FY27, and the maximum incentive is Rs. 1.2bn.
  • Why it has missed. On our proxy, renal revenue less the FY20 base, Polymed generated Rs. 500mn, Rs. 688mn, Rs. 1.2bn and Rs. 1.6bn of incremental sales in FY23-FY26, short of the threshold every year. Eligible sales may be defined differently.
  • Outcome. As of Jul-2026 Polymed had received no incentive, while Nipro had received Rs. 349mn. The MD had expected Rs. 400-450mn in 2021; by 2025 he answered "Zero" and said he was "building the business not on based on PLI".

Device regulation and reimbursement.

  • Dialysis machines are Class C devices under the Medical Devices Rules 2017. Licensing of Class C/D devices began in Oct-2023, which management credits for ending unregulated parallel imports.
  • The HDF machine faces a reimbursement ceiling: PM-JAY pays a flat per-session rate, so management expects HDF only in private centres, ~30-40% of the market.
  • The Parliamentary Standing Committee's CKD report recommends home peritoneal dialysis as first-line therapy. We would watch this, because Polymed's PD range is acute-care only.

Company-specific growth drivers, ranked

  1. Consumables pull-through from a larger installed base (management target; timing FY27-FY28).
    • Management plans a 20% rise in machine sales in FY27 and has a tender pipeline of more than 600 machines.
    • It has hired a renal head from Nipro, Fresenius and DaVita to work the chains and distributors.
    • Our view: the lever is conversion of PPP and chain tenders, where lumpy timing produced the FY26 miss.
  2. A trade-remedy duty on Chinese and Malaysian dialysers (event-driven; management expects a decision by end-2026).
    • A duty would let Polymed recover the volume it gave up in 1QFY27 without cutting price.
    • Our view: the outcome is binary for FY27 renal growth, and the exclusion of Fresenius brands limits the benefit to the low-price segment.
  3. Session growth and public funding (structural). F&S expects treatments to grow at a 14.3% CAGR, and PMNDP sessions have nearly tripled in five years. Every session consumes Polymed's needles and bloodlines whichever machine it runs on.
  4. A shift to single-use dialysers (management expectation). Moving from 30-35% to 50% single use would lift dialyser volume per session. Our view: chains' reprocessing economics and the absence of any reuse rule make this slow.
  5. New products (management target; 2026-2028). These are the HDF machine, 7-8 further renal products, and exports of renal products once capacity allows. HDF is ~10% of Indian dialysis and "dominated by large multinationals like Fresenius and Nipro".

Company-specific margin drivers, ranked

  1. Price, set by imports. The DGTR summary of Polymed's own injury claim describes losses, cash losses and negative ROCE on dialysers in CY25. That conflicts with the MD's May-2025 statement that renal was "not a loss making … the operating margin is positive" with PAT expected by end-FY26. The two cover different scopes (dialysers only versus the whole renal line) and periods, and we do not reconcile them. Management chose price over volume in 1QFY27.
  2. Duty inversion on inputs. Import content has fallen below 50%, but the 2.5% customs duty and 18% GST on inputs weigh against duty-free imports.
  3. Utilization. Capacity has doubled more than once since FY22 while revenue has been flat for five quarters. We infer under-absorption of plant and of the fixed service network until volumes recover.
  4. Mix. Machines, ~10% of renal revenue, are sold outright with no significant service income, and management declines to give product margins.
  5. Incentives. PLI has paid nothing so far; its remaining upside is capped at Rs. 1.2bn over the scheme life and needs thresholds that renal has not met.

What to watch

Open questions for management are in the question bank: the renal product split, dialyser volumes and reuse assumptions, machine margins, PPP tender wins, the basis of the share claims, and the reconciliation of the DGTR injury claim with earlier profitability statements.

A4.6 Anaesthesia, respiratory and critical care

This chapter covers two different businesses under one heading.

  • Anaesthesia and respiratory is an old, low-priced range of airways, circuits, masks, suction catheters and spinal needles that Polymed has sold for two decades. It was last disclosed at 2.9% of standalone turnover.
  • Critical care is a sales division set up in recent years. It bundles ICU devices from several product families (central lines, arterial catheters, midlines, vial-access spikes, Huber needles) and is one of management's two domestic growth bets alongside cardiology.

Neither has a revenue line in the financial statements or the investor decks.

[not disclosed]
Management ambition
Critical care to grow "almost 2 and 1/2 times" in FY26 (May-2025); Rs. 0.75-1.0bn of revenue in three to four years (Aug-2023)
Reach
20 plus critical-care products launched in a year; present in 500 hospitals (Nov-2025)
US
Class I respiratory and airway items listed with the FDA (exempt from 510(k))
What is disclosed
Occasional shares of turnover; no revenue, growth or margin for either business

What the range includes and how it is used

Two points on how the range is used.

  1. Demand follows surgery and ventilation. Surgery drives airways, circuits, HME filters and spinal needles. Ventilator-days drive suction catheters and circuits. Respiratory epidemics drive masks and nasal cannulas. In the second COVID wave (1QFY22) Polymed raised respiratory capacity "three to four times" within weeks and sold an oxygen Y-connector at Rs. 10.
  2. Critical care is a customer segment, not a product line. Its catalogue page regroups items also sold under infusion, vascular access and gastroenterology. Their revenue is therefore split across the BRSR buckets, and a separate "critical care" number would overlap with A4.1 and A4.2.

What is disclosed, and what is not

The FY26 BRSR drops the anaesthesia and respiratory line. Its FY25 share (2.9%) is close to the rise in the infusion share, from 67.1% to 69.9%, which suggests the line was folded into infusion. That is our inference; the company has not said so. The bases also differ: the placement-document series is consolidated product sales, the BRSR is standalone turnover. The two show a business that has grown roughly in line with the group rather than faster than it.

Critical care: the growth project

Management's account of critical care has moved:

  • Launch date. The FY26 annual report dates entry to 2019. The placement document calls it a division launched in FY23, and the FY25 call says "started FY25".
  • Scale claims. By Nov-2025 Polymed had launched 20 plus critical-care products in a year and was present in 500 hospitals, including top-tier chains. 6 new products were launched across infusion and critical care in 1QFY27.
  • Targets. In Aug-2023 management aimed for Rs. 0.75-1.0bn of critical-care revenue in three to four years "at a better margin". In May-2025 it hoped the segment would grow "almost 2 and 1/2 times" in FY26. Neither outcome has been disclosed.
  • Investment. Polymed added 70 people across cardiology and critical care in FY25, "with little contribution yet".

Why management likes the segment. It argues that critical care has few global competitors ("Cardiology ... 20 companies ... Critical Care is only 4-5 companies"). Indian demand is almost entirely imported (80-90%, Oct-2024), and ICU patients consume many devices each: management put ICU beds at ~20% of hospital beds. The segment is also the channel for oncology products (Section A4.2).

We read critical care as a cross-selling engine for devices Polymed already makes, sold by clinically trained staff, rather than a new product category. Its success should therefore show up in the domestic "others" line and in private-hospital growth, not in a separately reported number.

Market and competition

Market data are thin and vendor-based. Research and Markets pages put the global endotracheal-tube market at $2.54bn in 2026 and anaesthesia face masks at $252.42mn in 2025 (vendor estimates).

The multinationals are consolidating, and Chinese makers are widening their ranges:

  • Teleflex agreed in Dec-2025 to sell its Acute Care business to Intersurgical for $530mn, as part of a $1.5bn sale of its OEM unit and other divestitures. Acute Care covers airway management, anaesthesia, respiratory, humidification, oxygen therapy and regional anaesthesia. Teleflex had already sold respiratory lines to Medline in 2021.
  • ICU Medical, which bought Smiths Medical (Portex airway and tracheostomy products), reported Vital Care revenue of $437.9mn in CY25. That covers anaesthesia, respiratory, haemodynamic monitoring and regional anaesthesia, after most IV solutions moved to a joint venture. It names Intersurgical among its main Vital Care competitors.
  • BD and B. Braun are strong in regional anaesthesia: BD sells spinal and epidural needles and trays in its Medication Delivery Solutions unit, and B. Braun cites regional anaesthesia as a growth driver of its Hospital Care division.
  • BD in critical care. In Sep-2024 BD bought Edwards Lifesciences' Critical Care group for $3.9bn and renamed it Advanced Patient Monitoring. Its range includes arterial pressure monitoring products and pulmonary artery catheters, so the largest infusion competitor now also sells the monitoring systems that Polymed's arterial cannulas and catheters connect to.
  • Chinese makers are registering the same basic items in Europe: KDL completed CE registration for 22 products in CY25, including suction, feeding and urinary catheters.

In India, management says imports supply most of critical-care demand. CRISIL notes that Indian makers mostly produce basic items such as nasal oxygen cannulas, oxygen masks, ventilator circuits and mucus extractors, and that multinationals and imports dominate the consumables market.

Two domestic rivals show the competition in that basic range. Romsons sells anaesthesia, respiratory, urology and transfusion disposables; 1Lattice puts its FY24 revenue at Rs. 8.6bn and its EBITDA margin at 26.8%, and Temasek took a minority stake in it in Sep-2026. Angiplast makes nasal oxygen cannulas and oxygen and nebulizer masks and says it exports more than 80% of its output.

Polymed's position in the basic range rests on price and breadth within the same distributor basket as infusion. In critical care it rests on local manufacture against imports and on clinical selling. We see no evidence of a share lead in any single product here.

Regulation specific to the line

  • US. Polymed's FDA device listings include Class I respiratory and airway items that need no 510(k): tracheobronchial suction catheters and a suction catheter kit (Jaipur), nasal oxygen cannula, breathing circuit, oropharyngeal airway, and oxygen and venturi masks (Faridabad). These can be sold in the US without clearance. The suction catheter kit is listed under the proprietary name "McKesson", a US distributor, which points to private-label supply (Section A4.10).
  • India pricing. In 2014 the NPPA alleged that Polymed charged 20% above the maximum price on spinal needles. It demanded Rs. 9.3mn, of which Rs. 1.8mn was paid under protest. The contingent liability (Rs. 6.7mn) was shown in the FY25 accounts as since disposed of. The Maharashtra FDA survey reported in Sep-2026, which named a Polymed IV set, also found a nebuliser marked up 1,688% (maker not named); the consultation on trade margins ordered that month would cover respiratory consumables too (Section A4.1).
  • Europe. Most of the range is low-risk under the MDR, but re-certification of each variant still costs time. Management said Polymed had to drop products during the MDR transition (Section A4.1).

Growth and margin drivers, ranked

  1. Critical-care cross-selling in Indian private hospitals (management target; our view: plausible but unmeasured). The levers are import substitution and clinical sales staff. It is measurable only through domestic growth.
  2. Surgical volumes and caesarean-heavy spinal-needle demand (our view). This is the base-load driver of the anaesthesia range.
  3. Export of Class I items to the US (our view: small). Polymed already lists them, and private label is one route.
  4. Margin (our view). Anaesthesia and respiratory items are commodity-like, and we read them as earning below the group average. Critical-care devices replace imports and management says they carry "a better margin". Neither margin is disclosed.

What to watch

Open questions for management (also in the question bank):

  • where the anaesthesia and respiratory line went in the FY26 BRSR;
  • critical-care revenue, and how it overlaps with vascular access;
  • whether the FY26 "two and a half times" growth ambition for critical care was met;
  • US private-label volumes of Class I respiratory items.

A4.8 Cardiology

Cardiology at a glance

Revenue 1QFY27
Rs. 286mn, 5% of consolidated revenue (vs Rs. 29mn and 1% in 1QFY26), up 897% yoy on the PendraCare consolidation
What it includes
India-made drug-eluting stents (DES), balloons, catheters, guidewires and cath-lab accessories; PendraCare (Leek, Netherlands) from 23 Sep 2025
FY26 revenue
[not disclosed]; the MD put FY26 stent sales at Rs. 100-120mn; PendraCare added Rs. 442mn after acquisition
Stents implanted
~13,000 units cumulative by Jul-2026 since the Mar-2025 launch (our unit conversion of the company's figure)
Clinical evidence
PACIFIER DES registry: 840+ of 2,000 patients enrolled by Aug-2026
PendraCare deal
An enterprise value of €18.3mn (press release) to €18.8mn (1QFY27 deck), 13x CY24 EBITDA (company); CY25 EBITDA ~€84k
Management target
Rs. 3-4bn of cardiology revenue by 2030 and 5-7% of the business within five years (Oct-2024)
Not disclosed
The split between PendraCare and the India business, revenue by product, segment margins

Cardiology is Polymed's first move out of rupee-priced disposables into cath-lab devices that sell for thousands of rupees each, and it now carries its own revenue line. The line is still small, at 5% of 1QFY27 revenue, and its two engines are both running below plan. In-house DES volumes in FY26 were about half of what management planned. PendraCare, bought in Sep-2025, saw its EBITDA fall from €1.4mn in CY24 to ~€84k in CY25. We see the value of the line in the accessory basket and in drug-eluting balloons (DEB) and intravascular lithotripsy (IVL), where imports dominate. We see less of it in the stent, where prices are capped and Indian makers already lead.

What the devices do and the unit of demand

A coronary angioplasty (percutaneous coronary intervention, PCI) consumes a basket of devices.

  • Access: an arterial needle and an introducer sheath.
  • Delivery: a guiding catheter seated at the mouth of the coronary artery, and a guidewire run through it.
  • Treatment: semi-compliant balloons to open the narrowing, a stent to hold it open, and non-compliant balloons to expand the stent fully.
  • Accessories: an inflation device, a Y-connector valve and a manifold, often sold together as a kit.

A diagnostic angiogram needs diagnostic catheters and wires only. A DEB delivers drug to the vessel wall without leaving a stent, and IVL cracks calcified plaque before a stent is placed. The unit of demand is therefore the procedure. Management estimates that India performs ~700,000 angioplasties a year and uses ~1.3mn units of coronary stents, or 1.6-1.7 stents per patient. It puts annual sales at ~50,000 units for DEBs and ~10,000 units for IVL.

Polymed's range: a full cath-lab basket, built in two years

Polymed entered cardiology in 2024 with a soft launch at Arab Health. Its DES licence came in Feb-2025 and the stent went on sale in Mar-2025. DCGI approved its DEB and IVL systems in 3QFY26. By the Sep-2026 AGM the DEB was on sale and the IVL system was "soon launching". Management says both were developed on its own R&D platform.

Who makes which device is [not disclosed]. No legal manufacturer is printed on any ordering table or product page, so we cannot tell which items come from Polymed's plants, which from PendraCare and which are bought in. The Nov-2024 components catalogue already offered a cobalt-chromium stent in sirolimus and everolimus versions, together with diagnostic catheters and guidewires, as parts for other device makers. Frost & Sullivan's Jul-2025 report for Sahajanand Medical Technologies (SMT) still listed Polymed only as a PTCA-balloon maker "most focused on consumables".

Traction: stent volumes, the registry and the approval clock

Cumulative deployments reached ~11,000 units by 30 Apr 2026, so FY26 volumes were roughly half of the close to 20,000 units management planned in Aug-2025. Management says the stent is a small business, worth Rs. 100-120mn of FY26 revenue. It uses the stent as a door-opener for diagnostic catheters, guidewires and balloons. The stent is still sold mainly outside the top-tier hospitals, which management says it has not yet entered.

The PACIFIER registry is the evidence base for taking the RisoR stent abroad.

  • Design: 2,000 patients (1,960 in India and 40 in Europe) at 50 Indian sites and one in Italy, with imaging sub-studies of 100 (QCA) and 50 (OCT) patients, over 24 months. It is an open-label, single-arm registry, which management describes as post-market evaluation in India and "pre-market readiness" for Europe.
  • Enrolment: 200+ patients by Feb-2026, 650+ by May-2026 and 840+ by Aug-2026, against a target of full enrolment by end-FY27. The design had assumed a one-year enrolment window.
  • Our arithmetic: at the Feb-Aug 2026 pace of ~107 patients a month, the remaining 1,160 take ~11 months, which runs past end-FY27 (our calculation). Data follow at least a year after the last implant, and management says Class III implants take 3-5 years to win approval in global markets. We therefore do not expect European sales of the RisoR stent before FY29.
  • Disclosure quality: the 4QFY26 deck printed 2,000+ patients enrolled on one slide and 650+ on another.

PendraCare: what Polymed bought, and what has happened since

The deal. Polymed bought 90% of PendraCare Holdings and Wellinq Medical from Wellinq Holdings. The buyer was Risor Holdings BV, which is owned by Poly Medicure BV.

  • Price: an upfront equity payment of €11mn plus €3.2mn of inter-company loans repaid, a total of €14.2mn. Polymed also took on €2.9mn of net debt.
  • Valuation terms: an enterprise value of €18.3mn at first closing, or €18.8mn in the 1QFY27 deck. That is 1.8x CY24 revenue and 13x CY24 EBITDA (company).
  • Deferred terms: milestone earn-outs run over 4-5 years. The CEO's remaining 10% is bought in 2030 at a price set on calendar 2029 EBITDA; neither amount is disclosed.
  • Accounts: the annual report records Rs. 1.5bn paid in cash and Rs. 314mn of contingent consideration, with provisional goodwill of Rs. 1.6bn.
  • Funding: Rs. 1.5bn came from the Aug-2024 QIP and was lent on to Risor by Poly Medicure BV (€14.6mn at a floating rate linked to Euribor).

The business. PendraCare was founded in 2011 and describes itself as one of the few independent makers of interventional-cardiology catheters.

  • Products: guiding catheters were 79% of CY24 core revenue and diagnostic catheters 21%. It also sells semi-finished catheter parts and designs and makes braided catheters for other companies.
  • Channel: 48% of revenue came from OEM customers and 52% from its own brand, sold through 50+ distributors in 35+ countries with no direct sales force. Its OEM relationships with 2 large device companies go back more than a decade.
  • Regulatory assets: registrations in 60+ countries and 4 US 510(k)s, the latest for the SimplGuide introducer in Jun-2026. Its guiding catheter has 2.5 years of ARCUS-IMPROVE clinical data.
  • Plant: 3,800 m² across three leased sites in Leek with 1,150 m² of clean room. Capacity is 1.5 mn units/year against production of 700-800 thousand units. The staff is 65+ people.

Four points stand out.

  1. The CY25 collapse. Revenue fell 17.2% and EBITDA margin went from 14.1% to 1.0% (our calculations; the AGM deck prints CY25 gross profit of €6.3mn, not ~€5.59mn). The company has not explained the fall. On the 1QFY27 call management pointed to an "over-indexed" exposure to West Asia of about 20-odd percent. It said the business is "currently not growing", has withheld FY27 guidance for it and has not disclosed its 1QFY27 growth.
  2. The post-deal accounts are worse than the deck. Over the roughly six months after the deal, Risor's consolidated revenue of €4.17mn did not cover costs, and employee cost alone ate 65.6% of it. EBITDA was a loss of €752k and the net loss €1.33mn (our calculation from the unaudited accounts). Risor was set up with €20k of share capital and funded by the Poly Medicure BV loan, so the loss turned its equity negative. In the consolidated accounts, PendraCare added Rs. 442mn of revenue and a pre-tax loss of Rs. 141mn.
  3. Targets are far from delivery. Management promised €3-4mn of annual EBITDA synergies within three to four years, and revenue of close to €25mn by 2030 including new neuro and structural-heart products. CY25 EBITDA of ~€84k makes both look distant.
  4. Housekeeping conflicts. The EV is printed as €18.3mn, ~€18mn and €18.8mn in different documents. Risor's incorporation date is 29 Aug 2025 in the annual report but 4 Nov 2025 in Poly Medicure BV's notes, after the Sep-2025 loan to it.

The integration plan has four parts.

  • Move manual process steps to India; management said this was at the regulatory-approval stage in Aug-2026.
  • Consolidate the three Leek sites into one ~2,300 m² lease in calendar 2028. The new site will need its own approvals.
  • Start US sales of the guiding catheter in FY27 through distributors and a global OEM.
  • Register PendraCare products for import into India, which management says takes 6-9 months.

Market: a price-capped stent market and an import-heavy accessory market

Three features of the market shape Polymed's opportunity.

  1. Stents are price-capped. NPPA's 2017 cap cut patient prices by 60-80% according to CRISIL, and by 85% according to Frost & Sullivan. Price increases since then have been limited to the wholesale price index.
  2. Indian makers already hold the stent market. Management puts the Indian share at 70% today, against 10% a decade ago, while Frost & Sullivan says about 60%. A new entrant therefore wins stent share on price or service, and management concedes that peers "already have clinical trial data". The import-dependent parts of the basket are catheters, specialty balloons, DEB and IVL.
  3. Procedures should keep growing. India performs a small fraction of rich-country PCI rates per head, and 200-250 cath labs are added each year. Management says the stent market has "almost doubled" in five years, and expects DEB and IVL volumes to grow 2-3-fold in three to five years.

Globally, Frost & Sullivan's report for Integris sizes interventional cardiology at $14.3bn in 2024. It puts catheters at $3.6bn, growing 10.6% a year, and PTCA balloons at $2.9bn. The same firm's report for SMT gives $1.3bn for PTCA balloon catheters, which shows how much these vendor figures depend on definitions.

Customers, channel and pricing

  • India: Polymed sells to cath labs through its own field force and distributors. It added 70 people to cardiology and critical care in FY25 and trains cardiologists at its PACE academy.
  • Price points: the DEB and IVL carry ASPs above Rs. 115,000, against a stent price of Rs. 10,000-12,000. Management says pipeline products will be priced between Rs. 100,000 and Rs. 1.0mn.
  • PendraCare: it sells through distributors and OEM partners. Management rules out a direct sales force for now and plans to put PendraCare products into Polymed's Indian sales bag.

Competition

  • Stents: Abbott, Boston Scientific, Medtronic, Teleflex, Biosensors and Terumo hold over 90% of the global DES market.
    • In India the leaders are SMT (~25% of DES volumes), Integris/Translumina (~22%), Meril, Micro Life Sciences and Relisys.
    • The MD calls Meril the one Indian peer with a comparable spread of businesses, and notes that it entered cardiology more than a decade before Polymed.
  • Accessories, DEB and IVL: Frost & Sullivan's Oct-2025 list shows that Integris already sells guiding and diagnostic catheters, guidewires, inflation devices, introducer sheaths, Y-connector kits and coronary IVL. Polymed is therefore not alone in the import-substitution play it describes.
  • Guiding catheters worldwide: PendraCare competes with the large multinationals, some of which also buy from it as OEM customers. Management counts several times as many competitors in cardiology as in critical care.

Regulation

  • India: DES and bare-metal stents sit under NPPA ceiling prices. Other cath-lab devices do not, but their MRPs are subject to the annual price-increase limit that DPCO Para 20 sets for notified devices (Section B3).
  • Europe and the US: management says approvals for implantable devices take years and that EU MDR has made them "extremely challenging". It called PendraCare's CE and FDA clearances the main reason to buy rather than build. Polymed's own cardiology devices have no US 510(k); the group's cardiology clearances all belong to PendraCare.

Capacity and supply chain

  • India: cardiology capacity will move to a new plant on a plot of 7.2 acres in the YEIDA Medical Devices Park near the new Noida airport, where commercial production is guided for 1QFY28 (Section A6).
  • Netherlands: PendraCare runs at about half its capacity, and management puts both acquired businesses at 50-60% of capacity.

Growth drivers, ranked

  1. DEB and IVL (management target, FY27 onward). These products are import substitutes priced above Rs. 115,000, sold into a market of ~50,000 units of DEBs and ~10,000 units of IVL systems a year that management expects to multiply. We rank this first because the ASP is high and India has few local suppliers, though Integris is ahead in IVL.
  2. Basket pull-through (our view). A catheter, wire, balloon and kit accompany every stent. Winning top-tier hospitals would lift revenue per procedure more than stent volume would.
  3. PendraCare in the US and as a contract maker (management target, FY27). The guiding catheter is cleared and sales are expected from FY27. This depends on the OEM partner, which is not named.
  4. RisoR abroad (our view, FY29 at the earliest). This depends on completing PACIFIER, a year of follow-up and a European approval.
  5. YEIDA capacity (1QFY28, management guidance). The plant matters only if demand catches up with the stent plan.

Margin drivers, ranked

  1. PendraCare's recovery. It moved from a 14.1% EBITDA margin (CY24) to 1.0% (CY25). Management says the combined acquired businesses run at 12-14% and can reach 18-20% in two to three years through India engineering, global procurement and shifting manual steps to India.
  2. Mix. DEB, IVL and PendraCare's gross margin (73.7% in CY24) sit well above capped stents.
  3. Front-loaded costs. The registry, clinical teams and a new sales force are expensed ahead of revenue, and the government has granted Rs. 33mn towards clinical studies.
  4. Euro translation for PendraCare.

What to watch

Open questions for management are in the plant-visit question bank (Part C). They include which cardiology devices are made in-house, PendraCare's CY25 EBITDA bridge and the terms of the earn-out.

A4.9 Orthopaedics (Citieffe)

Orthopaedics at a glance

Revenue 1QFY27
Rs. 492mn, 9% of consolidated revenue, in the first full quarter of consolidation
FY26 contribution
Rs. 726mn of revenue and a pre-tax loss of Rs. 1.0mn from 7 Nov 2025 (annual report)
Citieffe CY25
Revenue €17.7mn and EBITDA ~€3.15mn (company); IFRS net loss €1.21mn
Deal
An enterprise value of €31mn, 10.2x CY24 EBITDA (company); closed 6 Nov 2025
Products
Trauma and extremity fixation: intramedullary nails, external fixators, screws, a wrist plate and a navigation system; 11 US 510(k)s
Sales mix CY25
Europe 48.3%, US 16.9%, rest of world 34.8%
Management targets
Revenue growth of 10-12% in euros in FY27; revenue of €25-30mn within about five years (Sep-2025)
Not disclosed
Citieffe's 1QFY27 growth and margin, revenue by product, prices

Citieffe gives Polymed a complete trauma-implant franchise with its own brand, EU MDR and US clearances and direct sales teams in three countries. What it does not yet give is growth or profit. Revenue was flat in CY25 and the group made an IFRS net loss. It carries interest-bearing debt about equal to its equity, and 51% of its receivables are more than 120 days old. The investment case rests on three steps management has yet to take: 1) adding plates, 2) building a larger US sales team, and 3) moving part of production to India.

What it is and how it is used

Citieffe makes implants that hold broken bones in place while they heal.

  • Intramedullary nails: metal rods run down the hollow centre of the femur, tibia, humerus or fibula and locked with screws. This is the standard fix for many long-bone shaft fractures.
  • External fixators: frames outside the limb, attached to bone by pins, for open or complex fractures and limb reconstruction.
  • Screws and plates: cannulated screws for fractures such as the femoral neck, and plates for fractures such as the wrist.

The unit of demand is the fracture: one nail and its locking screws per long-bone fracture, or one frame per complex fracture. The pins and screws are single use, while frame parts are re-used in some markets. Implant sets usually reach hospitals on consignment with instrument trays, and the navigation system is placed with hospitals to support nail sales. Trauma surgery cannot be postponed. Industry data in the acquisition deck show the trauma and extremities market fell 6.1% in the Covid year, against 11% for orthopaedics as a whole.

Citieffe's portfolio and position

  • Company: Citieffe was founded near Bologna in 1962 and has been run since 2019 by CEO Pascal Govi, who has 34 years of experience. It holds 45 patents, has an R&D team of 6 FTE spending ~5% of revenue, and launches 3-5 products a year. It reports a very low defect rate.
  • Position: it is the number-two independent player in Italy with a share of ~12% excluding plates, and one of the top players in Mexico with ~12% excluding plates and low-cost products. Both are company estimates.
  • Reach: ~85% of sales come from the three countries where it sells direct: Italy, the US and Mexico. It sells in 30+ countries in total. The distributor count is printed as 25+ in the 1QFY27 deck but 50+ in the annual report.

The deal

The deal was signed on 24 Sep 2025, closed on 6 Nov 2025, and Citieffe was consolidated from 7 Nov 2025. The 10.2x figure is based on CY24 EBITDA of €3.1mn, which the company describes as excluding one-off expenses and income.

Financials: flat sales, a net loss and a long receivables tail

Five points stand out.

  1. Growth stalled. The company-presented revenue grew 2.3% in CY25, after 15% in CY24. Management said sales were flat because a tender Citieffe had won in Latin America was cancelled and pushed out. It guided 10-12% euro growth for FY27, but on the Aug-2026 call described Citieffe as growing at "mid- to high single digits".
  2. Two EBITDA figures. The company's EBITDA is ~€3.15mn for CY25. Adding back D&A and finance cost to the audited IFRS profit before tax gives €2.72mn (our calculation), and the same gap existed in CY24. We read the difference as the one-off items the company excludes. It matters because the price was set on the adjusted figure.
  3. The loss was mostly currency. The CY25 net loss of €1.21mn came after an FX loss of €1.26mn on the US and Mexican businesses. Interest fell to €423k from €659k. The CY24 profit also shrank in a restatement: the deferred tax asset on Citieffe Inc's US tax losses had been booked at the gross loss rather than the tax-effected amount, and the correction of €3.43mn cut equity.
  4. Receivables are stretched. 51% of gross receivables were more than 120 days old at Dec-2025, up from 44% a year earlier. The loss allowance covers only 24% of that overdue book (our calculations). Management says the acquired European businesses carry longer receivable cycles.
  5. Debt stays with the business. Interest-bearing debt of €13.1mn equals about 100% of equity (our calculation), backed partly by SIMEST and export-credit agency guarantees. Management puts the core loan at ~€9mn, repaid at €1.5-2mn a year. Italian overdrafts carry rates up to double digits.

Inside Polymed, Citieffe contributed Rs. 726mn of revenue and a pre-tax loss of Rs. 1.0mn between 7 Nov 2025 and 31 Mar 2026, and ~Rs. 430-440mn of 4QFY26 revenue. Management blamed part of the acquired businesses' ~Rs. 26mn EBITDA drag in 4QFY26 on Citieffe "selling certain low-margin products".

Market: trauma is the fastest-growing orthopaedic segment

  • Global: the acquisition deck puts orthopaedics at $61bn in 2024, growing 3.8% a year to 2028. Trauma and extremities is the largest and fastest-growing segment at $12bn, growing 6.3% a year to $16bn by 2028. Internal fixators are 82% of the segment and external fixators 13%, and the US is 67% of the orthopaedic market. Plates are almost 40% of the trauma market. These are vendor estimates quoted by the company.
  • India: the research firm engaged for G Surgiwear's DRHP (Dec-2025) values India's orthopaedic device market at $6.2bn in FY25, rising to $10.7bn by FY30 (11.4% a year), of which implants are $3.0bn. India is about 3% of the global market. These are vendor estimates.
  • Import dependence is disputed. CRISIL put implants at 80-90% imported in FY24, while management says 50-60% of orthopaedic implants are now made in India.

Customers, channel and pricing

  • Buyers: trauma surgeons and hospitals. Citieffe's own sales teams cover Italy, the US and Mexico, alongside 12 distributors in Europe and 50+ key opinion leaders worldwide.
  • US: Citieffe sells to trauma centres through independent agents rather than group purchasing contracts. Management ruled out selling Polymed's consumables through the orthopaedic reps.
  • Tenders: in Italian and Latin American public tenders a bidder often needs a full portfolio, which is the main argument for adding plates.
  • Prices: [not disclosed]; management declined to give product prices. Management put gross margin at 90%+ at the deal, while the 1QFY27 deck implies 68% (our calculation).

Competition

  • Multinationals: Stryker, DePuy Synthes, Zimmer Biomet, Smith+Nephew, Medtronic and Arthrex lead worldwide and in India's premium segment.
  • Indian makers: Meril, Sharma Orthopaedic, Narang Medical, Biorad Medisys and Bonetech sell cost-effective trauma, joint and spine implants.
  • Management's view: India has "a fairly large base of manufacturers" in trauma, and Zydus's recent French acquisition is mainly knee implants.
  • Citieffe's edge: Citieffe competes on design (its patents, navigation for nailing) and on a low complaint rate rather than on price, and it has no plates to offer in tenders.

Regulation

The whole Citieffe portfolio is certified under EU MDR. Its products are Class IIb in Europe and Class II in the US. Registration in India's import regime takes 6-9 months, according to management. India capped the MRPs of coronary stents and knee implants in 2017; trauma implants were not named in that order.

Capacity and supply chain

  • Plants: two sites in Bologna: a production plant of 1,000 m² with 12 machines, and an assembly and packaging site of 1,100 m² with 10 machines. They run at 60% of capacity, with room to add a third shift.
  • Sterilization: outsourced, with a plan to bring it in-house.
  • Capex: regular capex is €1.5-2mn a year including instrument sets, on a net block of ~€5mn. Management estimates the total invested in the business at ~€28-30mn.
  • Staff: 109 employees at the deal and 90+ in Aug-2026, although management says no staff cuts have been made at either acquisition.
  • India: at the deal, management said it had "no such plans" to move manufacturing to India, only to outsource parts of the process. By Aug-2026, moving manufacturing processes of both acquisitions to India was "at the regulatory approval stage". The new Palwal plant in Haryana, due online around Mar-2027, will focus on orthopaedics and transfusion (Section A6).

Growth drivers, ranked

  1. Plates (management plan, near term). Plates are almost 40% of the trauma market, and management says adding them doubles the addressable market and qualifies Citieffe for full-line tenders. No launch date or approval timeline has been given.
  2. US sales force (management plan). Citieffe has 10 US approvals with 8-10 more in the pipeline, and prices there are 4-5 Europe's. More agents should lift the smallest share of the sales mix.
  3. Polymed's distribution and an India unit (management plan, from FY27). This means registering Citieffe products for India and selling through Polymed's network in more countries.
  4. Recovery of the cancelled tender (our view). CY26 revenue should get a lift if the Latin American tender is re-awarded.
  5. Joint replacement (management plan, medium term). Spine is not in the stated plan.

Management's aim is to double the business within five years, to €25-30mn, "without any significant capex". That requires a growth rate well above the current pace.

Margin drivers, ranked

  1. India manufacturing. Management says the acquired businesses run at 12-14% EBITDA and can reach 18-20% within two to three years, through India engineering, global procurement and moving labour-intensive steps to India.
  2. Geographic mix. Each extra point of US sales carries prices several times Europe's.
  3. Product mix. Low-margin product sales hurt 4QFY26.
  4. Currency and financing. Currency swings on the US and Mexican units, and interest on €13.1mn of debt, sit below EBITDA but drove the CY25 loss.

What to watch

A4.10 Components, OEM and contract manufacturing

Polymed sells some of what it makes to other device companies rather than under its own name: finished products sold as private label, loose components and semi-finished parts, and, since 2025, design-and-manufacture contracts. The evidence is scattered, and the revenue is [not disclosed]. What we can piece together is that private label was ~28% of sales in FY22 and is concentrated in exports, that management wants it smaller, and that the acquired European businesses have brought a larger OEM share.

What Polymed offers other device makers

Components. The Nov-2024 components catalogue ("Empowering Healthcare Innovation") offers parts that another manufacturer can assemble, pack and sterilize under its own name:

  • catheters: diagnostic, CVC, haemodialysis, midline, mini-midline, PICC and anaesthesia conduction;
  • a coronary stent: cobalt-chromium with a biodegradable polymer, sirolimus or everolimus;
  • guidewires: nitinol straight and J-tip, stainless steel, PTFE-coated, hydrophilic, a nasogastric-tube guidewire and a guidewire advancer;
  • access parts: introducer needles (standard, safety and Y with valve), tear-away introducers and dilators;
  • infusion parts: Polyway stopcocks, flow regulators, T-connectors, and extruded tubing (radio-opaque, PVC-free, polyurethane, co-extruded).

Many of these items were in the components catalogue before Polymed listed them as branded cardiology products. The catalogue is therefore both a revenue line and a window into its capabilities.

The government has approved a grant of Rs. 100mn towards a Rs. 1.0bn Polymed project to make polymer tubing components for infusion therapy, bloodlines and dialysis accessories and central venous catheters (Section A4.1). That should deepen the extruded-tubing capability behind both the finished products and the components line (our view).

Private label. Finished products sold under a customer's brand, mainly abroad. The only documentary trace in the US is an FDA device listing at Jaipur for a suction catheter kit under the proprietary name "McKesson", a US distributor. Management says the US business will run through GPOs and distributors, with Polymed's role "limited to manufacturing in India".

Contract design and manufacturing (CDMO). In 1QFY26 Polymed signed two contracts, with a US company and a Hong Kong-headquartered company with large US operations. They cover new patented devices in vascular access and pain management, and 510(k) filings are in progress. Management expects revenue from FY27 and scale in "two, three years, four years".

Intra-group supply. Polymed supplies components to its subsidiaries, which management says creates "some margin creation at the India level". Sales to Plan1Health alone were Rs. 147mn in FY26.

The evidence on OEM and private label

Other sources add detail:

  • CRISIL Ratings wrote in 2023 that Polymed "supplies to other big players, such as Atroge and Asept" (names as printed). It said Polymed has "access to developed markets through contract manufacturing" but that India's low-cost image "limits the company's ability to command a premium".
  • Management's framing has shifted. The Oct-2020 deck pitched "new contract manufacturing opportunities". In May-2023 the MD said "Polymed doesn't have any contract manufacturing business today. And that's not our model". By 1QFY26 it had signed two CDMO contracts.
  • By market. Europe "is more favoured towards own branded", while the US leans to white label.
  • The acquisitions raise the OEM share. PendraCare makes semi-finished guiding and diagnostic catheter parts, licenses end-product finalization and does contract development and manufacturing of braided catheters for 2 large OEMs, with relationships of over 10 years. Plan1Health is "sole approved supplier to one of the largest OEMs for Class III implants".

The Vitromed Healthcare relationship runs the other way. Polymed pays this promoter-owned firm to make products on job work from Polymed's raw materials; it is not a customer. It is covered in Section A9.

Why it matters: margins, stickiness and concentration

  1. Margins. Private label usually sells below own-brand prices because the customer carries the brand and the selling cost, but Polymed does not disclose the gap. Management put export EBITDA at 30%+ in Feb-2023, against 18-20% for India (as transcribed, the answer sits inside the analyst's turn). Since exports carry nearly all the private label, the mix does not appear to have hurt export margins, but this cannot be tested.
  2. Stickiness. OEM supply is embedded in the customer's regulatory file: changing a component supplier means re-validation and often re-registration. Management says most of its customer relationships outside India run 15-20 years and that it has "hardly lost any large customer".
  3. Concentration. OEM revenue follows a few customers' production schedules. At group level concentration is low: the top ten customers were 29.0% of FY24 revenue and no single customer reached a tenth of sales (Section A2). The OEM customers are not named, so their weight within the top ten is [not disclosed].
  4. Strategic value. In Dec-2025 Teleflex agreed to sell its OEM business, which makes catheters, extrusions, introducers and guidewire-type components for other device makers, to Montagu and Kohlberg for about $1.5bn. That shows the OEM model can stand as a business in its own right. Polymed's components catalogue covers many of the same categories at a far smaller scale. India's CDMO opportunity is small today (<$100mn in 2025, per a study cited in the FY26 annual report) and is projected at $6-7bn by 2035.

We read Polymed's stance as pragmatic: own brand where it can build a franchise (India, Europe), private label and CDMO where access is otherwise hard (the US). The CDMO contracts are the first test of whether it can earn design fees, not just manufacturing margins.

Who else competes for OEM work

  • Chinese suppliers have long served the global majors. KDL, which ranks itself among China's ten largest exporters of polymer consumables, sells on OEM, ODM and own-brand terms and has long-term development and supply ties with several global device companies.
  • Chinese private label carries risk for the buyer. Jiangsu Caina made the syringes Cardinal Health sold in the US under its Monoject brand. The FDA found at least 41 US complaints, sent a warning letter and by May-2024 was telling users to move away from Caina's syringes.
  • Indian contract makers are smaller. Angiplast offers CDMO and OEM services and makes components such as spikes, injection sites, connectors and clamps, and says it exports more than 80% of its production. Lars Medicare calls itself a contract OEM supplier. Iscon Surgicals sold to OEMs as well as to government buyers.
  • The opening. CRISIL says that pricing pressure and supply-chain problems during and after the pandemic have pushed OEMs to seek cost-competitive alternatives, making India an emerging hub for devices of high complexity and medium volume.

Polymed's advantage over the Indian contract makers is its regulatory file: every plant is certified under the EU MDR and it holds 6 US 510(k)s (Section A4.1).

What to watch

Open questions for management (also in the question bank):

  • current own-brand and OEM shares, and the margin gap between them;
  • the names or types of the largest OEM customers, and their share of the top ten;
  • revenue from the components catalogue;
  • expected FY27 CDMO revenue and the status of the related 510(k) filings.

A5 Geographies and legal entities

Polymed is an Indian exporter first and a multinational second. 69% of FY26 revenue was earned outside India, yet only 11.3% came from foreign subsidiaries (our calculation). The rest was shipped from the Indian plants to distributors abroad. FY26 split the two apart: the holding company's own exports fell 3.2%, while the subsidiaries' sales rose 213% as PendraCare and Citieffe were consolidated (our calculation). We therefore treat international revenue as two businesses with different drivers:

  1. Indian-made disposables sold through distributors, which move with distributor stocking, tenders, product approvals, freight and Chinese pricing;
  2. acquired European device makers that sell partly direct to surgeons and hospitals, which move with clinical relationships, tender calendars and the euro.
