Where the revenue comes from

The annual report gives two views that together show where FY26 went wrong and where it went right.

  • Consolidated regions. Revenue is split into India, Europe and the rest of the world (RoW) in the MD&A and the presentations.
  • The holding company's exports. The consolidated notes split Poly Medicure Ltd's export sales into five regions and add the foreign subsidiaries' sales as a separate line.

Three points stand out.

  1. Europe is still the largest destination but lost share. Europe was 46% of the holding company's FY26 exports against 49% a year earlier (our calculation). Section A3 sets out the destocking, Chinese pricing and certification delays that management blamed (Exhibit 13).
  2. Asia was the only export region that grew (+15.9%, our calculation). The Asia line includes West Asia, where the Gulf conflict hit only in the last weeks of FY26.
  3. The Americas are the second-largest export destination (26% of exports). Latin America is the bulk of it: management has called LatAm its second-largest export market after Europe, and the US contributed less than $3-3.5mn of revenue in FY26 by management's account.

The regional mix has barely moved in two years: India, Europe and RoW each earn about a third of revenue, which the MD calls his long-run goal of 1/3 India and 2/3 RoW. That stability hides a change in how the non-Indian revenue is earned. In FY26 17% of revenue from outside India came from subsidiaries, with PendraCare and Citieffe consolidated for only part of the year; in 1QFY27 the two acquisitions alone were 19% of international revenue (both our calculations).

The legal structure: an Indian exporter, a Dutch holding company and the acquired businesses

The listed company in India owns the Indian plants and makes almost all group volume. Nearly everything abroad is held through Poly Medicure BV in Amsterdam, a holding and financing company with no employees. It received €42.8mn of new equity from India in FY26, which it used to buy Medistream (Citieffe) and to lend €14.6mn to Risor Holdings for PendraCare.

The acquisitions changed the balance sheet as much as the income statement.

  • Assets abroad. Non-current assets located outside India rose 16x in a year, from Rs. 170mn to Rs. 2.8bn (our calculation). They sit in Switzerland (Rs. 1.4bn, mostly the Medistream acquisition), the Netherlands (Rs. 691mn), Italy (Rs. 518mn), the US (Rs. 93mn), Mexico (Rs. 85mn) and China (Rs. 47mn of investment at cost).
  • Debt abroad. Bank term loans in the foreign subsidiaries were Rs. 681mn at 31 Mar 2026, all of it Citieffe's, at 1.5% to 3.12% plus 3M Euribor. The Indian parent has only working-capital debt.
  • Minorities. The Rs. 431mn of non-controlling interest is the sellers' retained stake in PendraCare, which Polymed can buy out by 2030 (Section A4.8).

What the table says about each part:

  • Plan1Health is the one foreign subsidiary that was already working. Its turnover rose 43% in rupees in CY25 (our calculation) and it made a profit in each of the three years. Section A4.2 covers it in detail.
  • PolyHealth is a support company, not the US business. Its revenue of $211k in FY26 (+102%, our calculation) is a small fraction of the US revenue that management puts at below $3-3.5mn, most of which is shipped from India direct to US distributors and group purchasing organizations (GPOs). It lost $346k in FY26, needed USD 375,000 of fresh capital from Poly Medicure BV, and its FY25 accounts carry a going-concern note that relies on parent support.
  • The acquired businesses made losses in their first months. Risor's post-deal loss and Citieffe's currency-driven CY25 loss are analysed in Sections A4.8 and A4.9. The ~Rs. 90mn one-off provision management booked in 4QFY26 'in one of our international subsidiaries' has not been attributed to an entity.
  • The China plant has shrunk into a loss (see Asia below).

Europe: distributors, a direct foothold in Italy and a regulatory reset

Europe is 32% of group revenue and the market Polymed built deliberately. Europe rose from 10-15% of exports around FY18 to almost 40% by FY22 after a Europe CEO was hired in 2017. Six Western European markets (the UK, France, Italy, Germany, Spain and Sweden) produced 80-85% of European revenue in May-2024.

How Polymed sells there. The Indian-made range goes through distributors: 75+ of them, with 82 products approved and 15 in the pipeline (May-2026). The acquired companies bring their own channels: Citieffe sells direct in Italy plus 12 distributors, PendraCare uses 17 distributors and 2 OEM relationships, and Plan1Health 20+ distributors. Italy, through Plan1Health and Citieffe, is the only European market where the group sells direct. The MD said in Aug-2026 that he wants to go direct in 3-4 more geographies, starting with new products, because 'our distributors only sell our existing products'.

What drives European revenue, in the order we rank them:

  1. Distributor stocking. European distributors normally hold 4-5 months of inventory; they cut it to 2-3 months in 2025, which management cited as a cause of the FY26 contraction alongside Chinese pricing and certification delays. The 1QFY27 organic growth of 17.6% came from 'new customer acquisitions' plus restocking. Management guided to 5-6 new customers from Apr-2026.
  2. Approvals under the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR). 89 products received MDR certificates, but management admits it 'had to drop many products initially' while waiting. The pipeline is 30+ products under registration and ~25 products due for CE marking within three to four months of Aug-2026. Under the EU's 2023 extension of the transition, legacy certificates run to 31 Dec 2027 for class III and implantable IIb devices and to 31 Dec 2028 for the rest, which matters most for Citieffe's implants and PendraCare's catheters.
  3. Chinese competition, now partly fenced off in public tenders. Management blamed 1HFY26 on Chinese product redirected from the US. Since 30 Jun 2025 the EU has excluded Chinese bidders from public medical-device tenders of €5mn or more and capped China-origin content at 50%; such tenders are ~59% of EU device procurement. Polymed's standalone business sells little through EU tenders today; the company names the acquisitions as its route into tender markets.
  4. Clinical selling. Polymed has hired more than 25 clinical staff to support distributors, after concluding that distributors 'are not able to do justice' to the clinical case for its products; it plans such teams in 25-30 markets. The MD's reasoning: to win on price alone 'I have to be 10% cheaper than China', which Polymed's scale does not allow.

The UK deserves separate mention. It was 5-6% of revenue in FY25, the National Health Service does ~90% of purchasing, and the India-UK trade agreement cut UK duty on most of Polymed's products from 4-5% to zero. Polymed bid for 6-7 new product categories, mostly vascular access, in the NHS's 2026 cycle and formed Poly Health Ltd to sell direct. The offset: NHS contracts slipped 1-1.5 years after the change of government.

United States: small revenue, a long approval queue and tariff whiplash

The US is the largest device market but a small Polymed market. Management guided US revenue of $2-3mn for FY25, said FY26 was below $3-3.5mn, and expects $3.5-4mn in FY27. The medium-term target of $15-20mn has kept its size but not its date: management called it a three-year goal in Jul-2024, three to four years in Oct-2024 and two to three years in Aug-2025.

The reasons it is still small, as management describes them:

  1. Approvals. The FDA database lists 6 510(k) clearances in Poly Medicure's name, all class II infusion devices (safety IV catheters and IV sets), the latest dated 1 Apr 2026. Management said in Nov-2025 that the FDA had started rejecting data from Indian test labs, so products had to be re-tested in the US and 'all work we have done in the past was negated'. It expected the new tests to finish by Apr-May 2026, re-filing to follow and new approvals from mid-2026.
  2. Channel. Polymed supplies through 4 distributors and GPO contracts ('two large GPOs and distributors'); 'our job is limited to manufacturing in India'. The FDA listing of a suction catheter kit at the Jaipur plant under the name of McKesson, a US distributor, is the only public sign of private-label supply.
  3. Tariffs. The US was 'a red flag because of ... tariff situation', which 'delayed our launch to the U.S. market quite a lot'.

The acquisitions give Polymed its first direct US presence. Citieffe sells to US trauma centres through its own reps and commissioned agents, not GPO contracts; the US was 16.9% of its CY25 sales, and management points to US orthopaedic prices of 4-5x Europe's. PendraCare's guiding catheter is cleared and management expects US sales to start in FY27.

West Asia: demand intact, shipments stuck

West Asia (the Gulf states and their neighbours) was 6-8% of revenue before the conflict that began in Feb-Mar 2026, by management's estimate. Management described demand as intact but called shipping 'a logistics nightmare': revenue from the region fell 32% yoy in 1QFY27, with 'all the orders ... still lying at ports or in factories'. That cut organic RoW growth to 4%.

  • Costs. Management said logistics costs rose 2-3 times in the six months to Aug-2026. Hapag-Lloyd added a war-risk surcharge of $1,500 per TEU, and Indian exporters faced 40-50% higher insurance on Gulf-routed cargo. The Drewry container index rose from $2,287 per 40ft on 2 Apr 2026 to $4,500 per 40ft on 17 Sep 2026.
  • The acquisitions add exposure. PendraCare had 'over-indexed exposure' of ~20% to the region, which management says is why it is not growing.
  • Recovery. Management expects West Asia to grow 20-25% once the situation improves. We would treat that as a rebound from a depressed base, not a trend.
  • Access. Saudi Arabia requires a marketing authorization and a licensed local authorized representative for every device.

Africa: a small export market, served partly through Egypt

Africa took Rs. 480mn of the holding company's FY26 exports, 4% of the total and -1.0% yoy (our calculation). Management has said Africa and South-East Asia 'don't contribute too much', and that the currency crisis of 2024 hit West Asia and Africa harder than Latin America. The Egyptian associate, which CRISIL describes as catering directly to 'the African and other markets', is Polymed's local manufacturing presence.

Latin America: Brazil goes direct

Latin America is Polymed's second-largest export region, with Brazil and Mexico growing and 'a good market share' in Argentina (May-2022). Registration is slow: management said in 2022 that registering a product in Mexico took almost two years.

Brazil is where Polymed is changing its model.

  • Market. Management sizes Brazil's device market at $13-15bn, the largest in South America. Brazil was the second-largest destination for India's exports of catheters, cannulas and needles (HS 901839) in 2025, at $46.7mn.
  • Rules. Under ANVISA's device rules of 2022, a registration must be held by a legal entity in Brazil and is valid for 10 years. A foreign maker selling through distributors leaves the registrations with them.
  • Moves. Polymed set up a Brazilian subsidiary in 1QFY26 (pre-operational; FY26 loss BRL 142k), then on 29 Apr 2026 bought Medyneo, a distribution company with ANVISA and import licences but no operations, for Rs. 3.4mn (about $40,000). Management says the purchase saves 18-24 months. Renato Rocha (ex-Descarpack, B. Braun and GE Healthcare) became CEO of Polymed Brazil in Aug-2026, and the Board has allocated funds for direct sales. The plan is to sell new products direct while distributors keep the existing range.
  • Mexico is covered by Citieffe's direct sales company, where Citieffe claims ~12% of its segment.

Asia: South-East Asia grows, the China plant winds down

South-East Asia is one of the two export markets management singled out for FY27 growth, alongside Europe. Polymed exhibited in Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Vietnam in 2025 and names the region in its go-direct plans. The competitive risk is that Chinese makers have built plants in ASEAN countries, which B. Braun describes as under 'enormous pricing pressure'; Weigao's Indonesian joint venture starts local production in the second half of 2026.

China. Poly Medicure (Laiyang) has been a wholly owned plant in Shandong since 2007. The MD described its purpose in 2022 as understanding Chinese technology, sourcing and 'making some critical components'. It is now shrinking:

  • Sales fell 31% in renminbi between FY24 and FY26 to RMB 8.82mn (our calculation); exports were only RMB 361k.
  • Margins. Gross margin fell from 26.2% to 21.5% (our calculation), and the plant made a net loss of RMB 526k in FY26.
  • Future. The MD said in Jul-2024 that the plant (fewer than 40-50 people, revenue under $2mn) would 'probably close' because Chinese costs are 'much, much higher' than India's and its ~20-year lease expires within 18-24 months. The business licence runs to 23 May 2027 and the FY26 accounts say an extension is 'in process'. The two statements conflict; we treat closure as likely but unconfirmed.

Egypt: a profitable associate that pays dividends

Ultra for Medical Products (Ultra Med) runs a plant of 12,500 sq m in Assiut making disposable devices. Polymed owns 23%; CRISIL describes it as a joint venture with the El-Agar group.

  • Growth. Sales in rupees rose 53% between CY23 and CY25 to Rs. 1.2bn (our calculation), recovering from the Egyptian pound's devaluation, which had cut CY22 sales to Rs. 736mn.
  • Profit. The associate's CY25 profit was about Rs. 249mn, a net margin of ~20% (our calculation from the AOC statement). Polymed's share, Rs. 57mn, is its only equity-accounted profit.
  • Cash and trade. Polymed received Rs. 33mn in dividend and governing-council share in FY26 and sold it Rs. 63mn of goods. The investment is carried at Rs. 152mn against a cost of Rs. 8.9mn.

India: the growth engine is the private hospital

India produced Rs. 5.8bn of revenue in FY26, up 19.6%, the fastest of the three regions. Management is deliberately shrinking government business in India.

  • Private vs government. Private customers were ~90% of domestic revenue in 3QFY26 and grew 22.5%. Government business (10-12%) fell 18%. Management's reasons are late state payments and tenders that do not reward quality. The target is 92-93% private and 6-7% government.
  • Coverage. Polymed reaches ~8,000 hospitals, against the ~20,000 larger Indian hospitals that management counts as addressable. The MD put coverage at 'one-third of the hospital[s]' in Feb-2025 and wallet share in covered hospitals at 5-7% in Nov-2025, having said below 20% earlier.
  • Channel. 650+ distributors in India and the group's 590+ direct reps. Management plans 100+ sales hires in FY27, uses ~Rs. 10mn of revenue a year per rep as a benchmark, and has ~40-45 clinical staff in India. Indranil Mukherjee (ex-B. Braun and Translumina) joined in 2026 as CEO for India and Asia-Pacific. The MD says 'you can see Polymed products in every top private chain in the country'.
  • Policy. The GST cut on devices (12% to 5% from 22 Sep 2025) lowered end prices, though management linked a 2QFY26 domestic slowdown to channel inventory adjusting to it. The larger risk is trade-margin regulation. A Maharashtra FDA survey in Sep-2026 cited a Polymed IV set bought at Rs. 10.5 with an MRP of Rs. 187, and a parliamentary committee has recommended capping the gap between landing price and MRP at 20% (Section B3).

Company-specific drivers by region, ranked

  1. Europe organic recovery and tender access (management target, partly visible). Mechanism: new customers, restocking, MDR approvals and the EU's exclusion of Chinese bidders. Evidence: 17.6% organic growth in 1QFY27. Timing: FY27. Our view: the most important swing factor for export growth.
  2. India private-hospital penetration (management target, visible). Mechanism: more reps, clinical staff and products per hospital. Evidence: private revenue grew 22.3% in 2QFY26 and 22.5% in 3QFY26. Timing: continuous.
  3. West Asia normalization (management expectation). Mechanism: pent-up orders ship once routes reopen. Evidence: none yet; -32% in 1QFY27.
  4. Direct models in Brazil and new European markets (management plan, early). Mechanism: own sales teams for new products. Evidence: Medyneo licences and a CEO hire; no revenue yet. Our view: a margin cost before it is a revenue gain.
  5. US (management target, repeatedly deferred). Mechanism: 510(k) re-filings and GPO contracts, plus Citieffe and PendraCare products. Evidence: $3.5-4mn expected in FY27. Our view: immaterial to FY27-FY28 revenue unless tariffs stay at 10% and the re-filed products clear.

Two margin effects follow. Direct selling raises gross margin but adds fixed sales cost ahead of revenue. The Gulf and container-freight shock raises delivered cost on the export business. Management raised prices at the start of FY27 to offset raw-material inflation, but has not said how much of the freight increase it recovers.

Open questions for management: revenue by country for the top ten markets; West Asia, US and Latin America revenue in rupees; PendraCare's and Citieffe's revenue by region; which subsidiary booked the 4QFY26 provision; whether the China plant closes or renews its licence; the cost and revenue plan for the Brazilian direct model; and the timetable for the next European direct market.

A6 Manufacturing, capacity and R&D

Polymed makes almost everything it sells, and it makes it in India. That is what lets it sell a cannula at a few rupees and still earn a mid-to-high-twenties operating margin. The process is integrated from mould-making to sterile pack: moulds, dies and much of the assembly machinery are built in-house, parts are moulded and extruded on site, and products are assembled on automated lines. Sterilization moved in-house in 2025. The next two years are about filling capacity rather than adding it:

  • capacity grew faster than output after FY22, and management puts utilization of the post-2021 capacity at 65-70%;
  • two new Indian plants (Palwal and the YEIDA medical-device park) and the second phase of the captive gamma sterilization plant come on stream between end-2026 and 1QFY28;
  • wages in Haryana, where most of the plants are, rose sharply from Apr-2026.

R&D spend is low by global standards at 1.6% of turnover but has grown 16% a year since FY19 (our calculation). It now supports 35 launches a year and a pipeline of more than 100 products.

Rs. 299mn (1.6% of turnover) in FY26; 399 patents; 35 launches in FY26
Not disclosed
Products and capacity by plant after FY24; share of output sterilized in-house; gamma plant cost and savings; whether needles are made in-house

The plants: what is made where

Polymed counts 15 facilities in 5 countries. India has 10, which includes the R&D centre, and the two Citieffe sites in Bologna count as one. The FY26 annual report lists nine Indian production units in three clusters: Faridabad in Haryana, Jaipur's Mahindra World City special economic zone (SEZ), and Haridwar in Uttarakhand. Plant-level product lists are not published. The table assembles what the calls, placement documents and the US FDA's registration database do reveal.

Three things in the table matter for a plant visit.

  1. The US plant is Unit II. All the FDA-cleared safety IV catheters are listed under the FEI at the export-oriented unit in Faridabad. The Jaipur SEZ, built for Europe, holds the only US private-label listing.
  2. Renal capacity sits at IMT and is running out. Management said current renal capacity lasts only to FY26-27, which is why renal capacity was part of the Palwal plan.
  3. The new plants are for the new businesses. Palwal is for orthopaedics, transfusion and infusion; YEIDA is for cardiology. Management expects partial revenue from the new capacity in FY27 and full revenue in FY28.

Capacity and utilization

The only plant-level capacity data are the chartered-engineer tables in the two placement documents (PD21 for FY18-FY20, PD24 for FY22-FY24). Since then the company has given only group totals in its presentations.

What the series shows:

  • FY24 was a capacity year. Installed capacity rose 20% in FY24 while output rose 6% (our calculation), as four plants commissioned in FY23-FY24 came on line. Utilization fell from 80.1% to 70.5%. The same placement document's MD&A gives 80.7% for FY24, a conflict it does not explain.
  • Presentation capacity has kept climbing: 1.2bn units (May-2023), 1.5bn units (Jul-2024), 1.8bn units (May-2025) and ~1.9bn units (Aug-2026). The presentations do not say which plants each figure covers.
  • Management's utilization statements are consistent with the certificates:
    • new plants start at 30-40%, take three to four years to reach 80-90%, and 80-85% is the practical peak;
    • in Oct-2024 the four new plants were at ~50%, existing plants at 75-80% and the blend at 60-65%;
    • in May-2026 capacity added since the 2021 QIP ran at 65-70%.

The acquired plants have the same slack: management put both PendraCare and Citieffe at 50-60% of capacity in Feb-2026. Group plant area rose from 63,000 sq m in FY20 to 95,000 sq m in FY26.

Automation, tooling and the machine shop

Every Indian plant has injection moulding (including hot-runner tools), extrusion, insert and blow moulding, and ultrasonic, UV and laser welding, with poka-yoke, vision inspection and servo controls. Each plant has its own effluent treatment plant. Moulds are made on in-house CNC machines, and much of the special-purpose assembly equipment is designed in-house. Management said these special-purpose machines take 12-18 months to deliver, which sets the lead time for new capacity.

We read the step from 200+ to 500+ assembly machines between Aug-2025 and Nov-2025 as a change in what is counted, not a purchase. The acquisitions added only 12 and 10 machines at Citieffe's two sites. The definition is a plant-visit question.

Needles. Polymed's devices depend on stainless-steel needles and cannulae. The sources do not say whether Polymed draws, grinds and siliconizes needles in-house or buys finished needles. Chinese competitors such as Kindly (KDL) run the full chain from tubing to assembled device, so this is a gap in understanding the cost position.

Job work. Not everything is made in Polymed's own plants. Standalone job-work charges were Rs. 1.0bn in FY26, of which Rs. 870mn (84%, our calculation) was paid to Vitromed Healthcare, a promoter-group firm that assembles products from materials Polymed supplies (Section A9).

Sterilization: from outsourced EtO to a captive gamma plant

Until 2025 Polymed sterilized mainly with EtO gas through third-party vendors. The catalogues label some products gamma-sterilized (the PolyFlush syringe, Polyswab, the ABG syringe) and others EtO-sterilized (transducer protectors, peritoneal-dialysis sets).

The captive plant has been a long project:

  1. May-2022. Management added Rs. 500mn to the capex plan for 'a controlled radiation plant', because many new products are gamma-sterilized, there was no facility near the plants, and outside vendors sometimes compromised quality. It was due in FY24.
  2. Jul-2024. Still under construction; management called gamma 'more safer' than the EtO 'which we use today' and planned to move 'most of our sterilization' to it.
  3. Aug-2025. Phase I started, licensed for Class A and B devices, with Class C and D licences awaited; source capacity to rise from 300 kci to 2,000 kci.
  4. Sep-2026. 'Operational; one of the few such captive facilities in India', with Phase II due by end-2026.

Management places the plant variously at 'Palwal' and at 'Faridabad-Mitral'; the annual report says Mitrol. Why it matters: EtO is under regulatory pressure. About 50% of US sterile devices are EtO-sterilized, and the FDA is encouraging alternatives including radiation. In-house sterilization should also shorten the time from moulding to shipment (our inference). Neither the cost of the plant nor the savings, nor the share of output now sterilized in-house, is disclosed. Citieffe outsources its sterilization and plans to bring it in-house.

Capex and the QIPs

The capex cycle has run in two waves, each funded by a qualified institutional placement (QIP):

  • 2021 QIP: four plants in FY23-FY24. They were a diagnostics plant in Faridabad, an extension of the export-oriented unit for the US, an IMT expansion for domestic and renal products, and an SEZ expansion for Europe. This is the capacity now at 65-70% utilization.
  • 2024 QIP: three plants. Rs. 5.0bn was earmarked for plants at Jaipur (Rs. 2.3bn), Palwal (Rs. 2.7bn) and Haridwar (Rs. 790mn), out of a total project cost of Rs. 5.8bn. The planned plant and machinery (Rs. 3.1bn) comprised assembly machines (Rs. 1.2bn), injection moulding (Rs. 679mn), tool room and moulds (Rs. 554mn) and clean rooms (Rs. 322mn); 99.7% of it had not been ordered at Aug-2024. Jaipur has since been replaced by YEIDA. By 31 Mar 2026 only Rs. 620mn (12%, our calculation) of the capex object had been spent, while Rs. 2.5bn of QIP money had gone to acquisitions. Section A9 covers the change of use.

Management says its asset turns 'remain between' 1.2-1.4x and expects that to continue. Reported fixed-asset turnover fell to 1.6x in FY26 as capacity ran ahead of revenue.

Workforce and wages

Headcount figures depend on the definition used. The annual report cites a group workforce of over 7,500 and an 'employee base' of 3,400+; the Directors' Report counts 2,614 permanent employees on the standalone rolls. The standalone BRSR gives the most complete picture.

Three implications:

  • Wage exposure is concentrated in Haryana. The Faridabad plants held 64% of group capacity in FY24 (our calculation), and Mitrol and Palwal are also in Haryana. Haryana raised minimum wages 35% from 1 Apr 2026, which management said drove a 29% rise in standalone employee cost in 1QFY27. The new Labour Codes cost a further Rs. 68mn provision in 3QFY26. Consolidated employee cost was Rs. 4.0bn in FY26.
  • Automation is the stated offset. Management said in May-2026 that it is 'pushing more on automation right now so that at least we can mitigate some wage revisions'.
  • Contract labour fell 28% in FY26 (our calculation) while permanent headcount rose. Whether this reflects automation, lower volumes or reclassification is not disclosed.

R&D, patents and launches

  • People. The DSIR-approved centre in Faridabad had 63 staff including 59 engineers in Jun-2024. The group R&D team was ~90+, including 45+ engineers across India, Italy and the Netherlands, in May-2026. R&D employee cost rose to Rs. 150mn, 50% of R&D expense (our calculation). Citieffe adds a team of 6 FTE.
  • Ambition. Vision 2030 promises to 'double R&D spend' (2x). Management puts spend at 1.7% of sales and says it will double in three to five years. Indian medtech firms spend 2-4% of revenue on R&D, per the industry study cited in the annual report.
  • Patents. The group holds 399 patents, of which 348 are Polymed's own, so the subsidiaries hold 51 (our calculation). Around 60 applications are pending. In FY25 the count was 334, including 116 in India, from 616 applications filed.
  • Clinical evidence. The 2,000-patient PACIFIER stent registry is the largest study Polymed has run (Section A4.8). The government granted Rs. 33mn for clinical studies of new import-substitution devices. Management uses contract research organizations for Class III devices and says companies typically spend 3-5 years getting global approvals for Class III implants.

Approvals by market

What drives plant economics, ranked

  1. Filling the capacity already built (visible). At 65-70% utilization on the post-2021 plants against a practical peak of 80-85%, volume growth can come with little new capex, which is why FY27 capex guidance is lower. Mechanism: fixed cost absorption. Timing: FY27-FY28.
  2. Wages against automation (headwind now). A 35% minimum-wage rise in the state that hosts most capacity is only partly offset by automation; the net effect showed up as 29% employee-cost growth in 1QFY27.
  3. Captive sterilization (management claim, unquantified). Management's stated aims are control of quality and turnaround and a safer process than EtO; we would add the vendor margin and transport it removes. The benefit is undisclosed and depends on the Class C/D licences.
  4. New plants for new businesses (cost before revenue). Palwal and YEIDA add depreciation and fixed cost from end-FY27, ahead of the orthopaedics and cardiology revenue they are built for.
  5. Moving acquired manufacturing processes to India (management plan, early). Citieffe's and PendraCare's plants run at 50-60%. At the Citieffe deal management had 'no plans' to move its manufacturing, only to outsource parts of the process to India; by Aug-2026 some process transfers for both acquisitions were 'at the regulatory approval stage'. Our view: a margin lever for FY28 onwards, gated by approvals.

Open questions for the plant visit are in the question bank (Part C): which products each unit makes; current capacity and utilization by unit; how assembly machines are counted; whether needles are ground in-house; the share of output sterilized in-house and its cost saving; and what moves to Palwal from Citieffe and PendraCare.

A7 What drives growth and margins: the driver maps

This section pulls together the company-specific drivers from the business-line chapters in Section A4. Each driver is labelled by its origin:

  • Management target: a figure or ambition management has stated.
  • Our view: our reading of the evidence, with the evidence shown.

Neither is a forecast. The ranking reflects how much each driver can move group revenue or margin over the medium term, on the disclosed evidence.

Growth drivers, ranked

Margin drivers, ranked

The standalone business earned an operating EBITDA margin of 26.8% in FY26 (our calculation), and management guides 25-27% for FY27.

The consolidated margin is lower, at 24.1% in 1QFY27 against 28% standalone, which management attributes to the lower margins of the subsidiaries.

The driver matrix by business line

The matrix sets out what drives each business line; the A4 chapters give the evidence.

A8 Competitive advantages and vulnerabilities

Polymed's advantage is a manufacturing one:

  • It makes high-volume disposables at a lower cost than Western majors and at a quality that clears European and US regulators.
  • It sells them through a distributor network in 125+ countries.

We see this as why the company earns margins in line with the best Indian peers while earning ~69% of revenue outside India. The weaknesses sit elsewhere:

  • Pricing power. It has little brand premium.
  • R&D depth. It spends 1.6% of revenue on R&D.
  • Chinese competition. It is exposed to Chinese makers with similar cost structures and larger scale.
  • The US. It is barely present in the largest market.

We read the acquisitions and the stated plan to double R&D spend as attempts to fix the second and fourth of these.

Where the advantage comes from

  1. Unit cost through automation and in-house engineering.
    • Polymed runs 530+ automatic assembly machines and 130+ robots. The presentations showed 200+ assembly machines from May-2022 to Sep-2025 and 500+ from Nov-2025; the company has not explained the step change. It fabricates its own moulds and develops and programs the robotics on its assembly lines in-house.
    • CRISIL attributes the company's operating margins to lower labour costs than global peers and to in-house tool design and R&D.
    • A peer comparison in Integris Medtech's draft offer document (Oct-2025) puts Polymed's FY25 EBITDA margin at 28.7% (gross margin 66.8%). That is the highest EBITDA margin among the companies it compares: Integris Medtech, Poly Medicure and Laxmi Dental.
  2. Scale in the core product. Management says Polymed is the world's #3 IV cannula maker, with about 11% global share and 600mn units a year. Scale spreads tooling, automation and regulatory costs over large volumes.
  3. Vertical integration.
    • The company makes components and moulds in-house and develops the automation on its assembly lines.
    • It commissioned in-house gamma sterilization in 2025.
    • It is India's first domestic maker of dialysers and, by management's account in May-2022, its only maker of prefilled flush syringes.
  4. Regulatory breadth.
    • 89 products carried EU MDR certification in FY25.
    • Products are registered in 100+ countries.
    • The company employs 200+ quality and regulatory professionals.
    • Polymed and its subsidiaries hold US 510(k) clearances in infusion (Polymed), pain management (Plan1Health), cardiology (PendraCare) and orthopaedics (Citieffe) (Appendix).

We see MDR as raising the cost of staying in Europe, which works against smaller suppliers (Section B4).

  1. Distribution reach.
    • 1,000+ distributors and 590+ direct-sales representatives.
    • No customer reaches the 10% disclosure threshold, and the top-10 customers were 29.0% of FY24 revenue.
  2. A steady launch cadence.
    • About 35 products new products in FY26 (including acquired ones), 390+ patents granted and a pipeline of 100+ products.

We read most organic launches as extensions of existing categories rather than new ones.

Where it is vulnerable

  1. Pricing power is limited.
    • CRISIL notes that India's low-cost image "limits the company's ability to command a premium".
    • In Europe, Polymed competes with Chinese makers of similar cost and larger scale. Weigao alone had revenue of RMB 13.4bn in CY25, 27% of it overseas.
    • FY26 showed how quickly redirected Chinese volume can reach European tenders (Section A3).
  2. R&D depth.
    • R&D spending is 1.6% of revenue, and we read the pipeline as broad but mostly incremental.
    • Management's answer is to buy technology and approvals, because organic development takes 3-5 years. That shifts the risk from R&D to integration.
  3. Under-penetration of the US.
    • Management expects US exports of $3.5-4mn in FY27. By comparison, BD's medication-delivery business alone had global revenue of $4.6bn in FY25.
    • Management says it has signed contracts with two large GPOs, but US scale also needs products tested and registered for the US; until then, we see little of the cost advantage reaching the largest market.
  4. Concentration in infusion and in Europe.
    • Infusion is still 53% of revenue.
    • The BRSR puts infusion therapy at 69.9% of standalone turnover on its broader definition.
  5. Imported inputs and labour intensity.
    • Most raw materials are imported.
    • Permanent-worker attrition was 74.6% in FY26, and 51.1% of permanent workers are paid the minimum wage.

Wage inflation erodes the labour-cost edge unless automation keeps pace.

What would strengthen or erode the advantage

Strengthen:

  • automation keeping employee cost flat as a share of revenue despite wage inflation;
  • the new plants lowering unit costs in renal and syringes;
  • FDA clearances and US contracts;
  • MDR-driven exits by smaller European suppliers;
  • trade remedies against dumped imports in India.

Erode:

  • Chinese makers relocating to Southeast Asia to escape US and Indian duties;
  • MNCs pricing aggressively in emerging markets;
  • a cap on trade margins in India;
  • slow integration of acquisitions that dilutes management attention away from the core franchise.

What to watch

A9 Management, governance and capital allocation

Polymed is a founder-run company. The Baid brothers built it and still run it, and the reported promoter group, which now includes two LLPs reclassified from the public category, holds 62.4% of the equity.

The strengths:

  • clean audit reports, with no auditor qualification in the five years to FY24;
  • a CRISIL rating of AA-/Positive;
  • a net cash balance sheet;
  • two QIPs that institutions absorbed.

Against these, we see five governance features that an investor should diligence before underwriting the FY30 plan:

  1. Job work with a promoter firm. Rs. 870mn of FY26 job work went to Vitromed Healthcare, a partnership of promoter-family members. That was 84% of all job-work charges (our calculation).
  2. A promoter group enlarged by reclassification. The reported holding moved from 44.7% to 62.4% after two LLPs that had been counted as public shareholders were reclassified. Neither step involved a purchase of shares.
  3. Promoter-family pay. It equalled 14.7% of standalone PAT in FY26 (our calculation), and the MD earned 497x the median employee.
  4. Slow deployment of the Aug-2024 QIP. Only 21% of the capex scheduled for deployment by FY26 was spent (our calculation), and the monitoring agency flagged that part of the idle money sat in hybrid mutual funds and a PMS.
  5. A mixed early record for the FY26 acquisitions. PendraCare contributed a pre-tax loss of Rs. 141mn in its first six months under Polymed, while Citieffe was close to breakeven after closing.

None of these is hidden. Each is disclosed in the annual report, the placement documents or the monitoring-agency reports. Institutions have not voted against the board in any number: no resolution at the 31st AGM drew more than 4.0% of institutional votes against, although none of the five items above was itself put to a vote.

Who runs Polymed

The operating company is still run by its founders:

  • Himanshu Baid (MD), who joined on 20-Sep-1996.
  • Rishi Baid (JMD), formerly with Miles Pharma in the US. Both describe themselves as first-generation entrepreneurs.
  • Their father, J.K. Baid, sits on the board as a non-executive director. Their mother, Mukulika Baid, stepped down from the board on 6-May-2025, the day Vishal Baid became an executive director.

The next generation is inside the business:

  • Vishal Baid is now an executive director, in charge of marketing, corporate finance and the Jaipur manufacturing operations.
  • Dhruv, Arham and Aaryaman Baid are employed in the company.

From 2025-26 a professional layer was added:

  • a CEO for India and APAC hired from Translumina, who earlier ran B. Braun in India;
  • a CEO for Brazil;
  • a head of the Indian renal business;
  • a President for strategy and corporate development.

The acquired businesses keep their own chief executives.

The board. At 31-Mar-2026 the board had 12 directors. Eight were non-executive, five of them independent, and one was an independent woman director.

  • Chairman. D.R. Mehta, a former SEBI chairman, has been on the board since 2005. He is now classified as a non-executive, non-independent director.
  • Re-appointment. Because he is older than 75 years, the 31st AGM re-appointed him by special resolution. 4.0% of institutional votes were cast against, the highest dissent of any resolution at the meeting.
  • Balance of the board. The four executive directors include three members of the promoter family. With the promoters' father and the Plan1 founder among the non-executives, the board has a slim independent balance by the standards of widely held companies. It still meets the one-third test that applies to a non-promoter non-executive chairman.

Shareholding: how the promoter group reached 62.4%

The promoter group's reported holding has swung between 44.7% and 66.0% over five years with almost no change in the family's own shareholdings. The swings are almost entirely the result of two reclassifications:

  • Zetta Matrix Consulting LLP. It held 9.4% in FY20 as a public shareholder and was moved into the promoter group in FY23.
  • Ezekiel Global Business Solutions LLP. It held 14.0% in FY20 and was listed as a major non-promoter shareholder through 31-Mar-2024. By 30-Jun-2024 it was inside the promoter group.

The arithmetic ties exactly:

  • The reported promoter holding at 31-Mar-2024 plus Ezekiel's then-public stake is 66.03% (our calculation). That is the promoter-group figure the placement document reported at 30-Jun-2024 (66.0%), weeks before the Aug-2024 QIP.
  • In FY20 the reported promoter group and the two LLPs together held 72.2%. In FY22 they held 66.2%. We attribute the fall between those years to dilution from the Feb-2021 QIP.

The documents we reviewed disclose neither who controls the two LLPs nor why they were reclassified. We therefore do not infer control. We do note three consequences:

  • The public float is 37.6%.
  • Public institutions held about 21.2% at the AGM record date (our calculation).
  • The effective free float is narrower than the pre-FY23 shareholding pattern implied.

Promoter shares carried no pledge at 30-Jun-2024.

Related parties: Vitromed and the family trust

Vitromed Healthcare is a Jaipur partnership of J.K. Baid, Rishi Baid, Vishal Baid and Polycure Martech Ltd, a company owned by directors and their relatives, according to the FY16 annual report; the FY26 report lists it among enterprises over which key management personnel and their relatives exercise significant influence.

  • Its role. It has been Polymed's main job-worker since at least FY09. It makes products and components from raw materials that Polymed supplies. It is not an OEM supplier.
  • Products. The Feb-2021 placement document named safety scalp-vein sets and silicone rubber sleeves among its products.
  • Two-way trade. Vitromed also buys goods from Polymed, so money flows in both directions.

Over time Vitromed's share of total job work has eased, but the rupee amount has grown 8.3x since FY10 (our calculation).

In FY26 the job work paid to Vitromed equalled 5.2% of standalone revenue (our calculation).

The transactions are disclosed every year:

  • Shareholders set contract caps of Rs. 600mn, Rs. 750mn and Rs. 900mn for FY19-21.
  • In FY10 sales to Vitromed exceeded the then Section 297 approval limit by Rs. 8.8mn.
  • We found no related-party approval resolution in the 2025 or 2026 AGM notices. The FY26 annual report states that all related-party transactions were at arm's length.
  • All FY26 dealings with Vitromed together equalled 5.9% of consolidated revenue (our calculation). That is below the materiality threshold in the company's policy – the lower of Rs. 10.0bn or 10% of consolidated turnover – above which shareholder approval would be needed.

We see two questions for management, both of which bear on margins:

  1. Is the pricing demonstrably arm's-length? The disclosures give amounts, not the terms or the margin Vitromed earns.
  2. Why is the capacity not brought in-house? The QIP funded new plants but did not absorb Vitromed.

CSR and the family trust.

  • Polymed routes a large share of its CSR spend through the Jai Chand Lal Hulasi Devi Baid Charitable Trust, a promoter-family trust: Rs. 21mn in FY26, or 51% of CSR spend (our calculation).
  • The trust received Rs. 3.0mn in FY21 and Rs. 21mn in FY24.

Other related parties.

  • Egypt associate. Ultra for Medical Products paid Polymed a dividend and governing-council share of Rs. 33mn in FY26.
  • Rent. Rent to promoter company Jai Polypan is immaterial.
  • Plan1 founder. Alessandro Balboni received business-development fees of Rs. 28mn in FY24.

Remuneration

Pay for the two promoter managing directors has two parts:

  • A fixed element. From 1-Aug-2024 basic salaries are Rs. 38mn for the MD and Rs. 37mn for the JMD, with annual increments of 8% and perquisites of 60% of salary.
  • A profit-linked commission of up to 5% of profits as computed under Section 198 of the Companies Act.

The ratio of the MD's pay to the median employee rose from 161x in FY16 to 579x in FY25. It eased to 497x in FY26, when the MD's pay fell 15.5% while the median employee's pay fell 1.6%.

  • Vishal Baid. His pay rose 372% in FY26 on his elevation to executive director.
  • Total promoter-family pay in FY26 was Rs. 493mn (our calculation).
  • ESOPs. The 2020 scheme grants options at an exercise price of Rs. 100, against the Aug-2024 QIP price of Rs. 1,880. The pool is 1,000,000 shares.

We read the scheme as a retention tool for the professional layer, since the promoters are not grantees. It is a deep-discount scheme, and its cost will show up as a share-based payment charge.

Capital allocation

QIP-2021 was deployed as planned. It raised Rs. 4.0bn in Feb-2021 with general objects and was fully used by 31-Mar-2023, Rs. 3.1bn of it on capex.

QIP-2024 is running behind on capex. The Aug-2024 QIP raised Rs. 10.0bn at Rs. 1,880 a share. Its objects were capex for new plants, inorganic growth and general corporate purposes.

  • The acquisition money went first, to PendraCare and Citieffe.
  • The capex money lagged. By 31-Mar-2026, Rs. 620mn had been spent on capex against Rs. 3.0bn scheduled for deployment by FY26.
  • Reason given. The company attributed the delay to moving the Jaipur SEZ project to the Medical Device Park on the Yamuna Expressway (YEIDA), and rescheduled the spend to FY27-28.
  • Idle money. Unutilized proceeds were Rs. 4.8bn at 31-Mar-2026 and Rs. 4.7bn at 30-Jun-2026.

The monitoring agency's 4QFY26 report added a sharper point:

  • It flagged that Rs. 719mn of unutilized proceeds had been placed in hybrid mutual funds with equity exposure (market value Rs. 759mn), and that Rs. 50mn was in a Nuvama absolute-return PMS.
  • It called the hybrid-fund placement "not in line with the disclosures made by the Company in the Placement Document".
  • The board's recorded comment was "No Comments".

We view the amount as small, but the episode is a data point on treasury discipline.

Acquisitions. The acquisition record is short and mixed. Plan1 has grown into a profitable if small business. PendraCare lost money in its first six months under Polymed. Citieffe was close to breakeven after closing, although its CY25 statutory accounts show a net loss driven by an FX loss. Integration of both is only beginning. Management has said it wants to "pause and absorb".

Its stated M&A criteria are unchanged:

  • technology and regulatory approvals in adjacencies chosen by disease burden: renal, cardiology, critical care, oncology and orthopaedics;
  • buying time, because organic development takes 3-5 years.

Cash and payout. Polymed ended FY26 with net cash of ~Rs. 5.0bn and liquidity of Rs. 8.0bn+.

  • Other income. Other income is a large part of profit: it was 28% of consolidated PBT in FY26 (our calculation). At the standalone level it included realized and unrealized mutual-fund gains of Rs. 402mn and Rs. 126mn and FX gains of Rs. 381mn.
  • Payout. The dividend was Rs. 3.5 a share, a payout of 11% of consolidated PAT (our calculation).
  • Management's rationale. In May-2025 it justified a lower payout by heavy capex and M&A opportunities.
  • Returns. Consolidated ROCE fell to 16.4% in FY26 from 23.5% on the company's adjusted definition, which already excludes unutilized QIP money from capital employed; we infer that the acquisitions entering the capital base, with their low early profits, explain most of the fall.

We see capital allocation, rather than the operating franchise, as the swing factor for returns through FY28:

  • the unspent plant capex at YEIDA, Palwal and Haridwar;
  • the turnaround of two loss-making acquisitions;
  • what happens to about Rs. 4.7bn of unused QIP money.

Audit, litigation and contingent items

Auditors.

  • Doogar & Associates audited Polymed until FY19. M.C. Bhandari & Co. took over from the 2019 AGM.
  • Doogar & Associates were re-appointed at the 29th AGM on 26-Sep-2024 for a term to 2029.
  • The placement document reports no auditor qualifications and no material frauds over the preceding five years.

Credit. CRISIL moved the outlook to Positive in Jun-2026.

  • Upgrade trigger: revenue above Rs. 22.0bn with an operating margin of 22-24%.
  • Downgrade trigger: a sustained margin below 20%, or larger-than-expected capex or acquisitions.

Total contingent liabilities listed in the FY26 annual report were Rs. 88mn (our calculation), against Rs. 535mn at 31-Mar-2024.

Most of the difference is the Rs. 424mn CGST show-cause notice. The disclosures do not say whether it was settled, dropped or reclassified, so we list it as a question for management.

What to watch

Questions for management raised by this section feed the plant-visit question bank in Part C.

Part B – The industry

Part B describes the industry around Polymed: how disposables are bought and priced (B1), who it competes with (B2), the Indian market and its policy (B3), the regimes in its export markets (B4) and the structural trends that will reshape all of them (B5). Markets for individual product lines sit in the A4 chapters. Market sizes from commissioned industry reports and market-research firms are vendor estimates and are labelled as such.

B1 How medical disposables are bought and priced

A disposables maker does not set its price so much as meet the price of whoever buys: a US group purchasing contract, a European hospital tender, a distributor in an emerging market, a Chinese volume-based tender or one of India's three domestic channels. Each has a different decision-maker, contract term and price mechanism. That explains three things about Polymed:

  1. why the same device sells at very different prices by region (Section A4.1 gives the MD's example of one BD product at $1 in Europe, $3 in the US and $0.25 in Africa);
  2. why a customer, once won, tends to stay;
  3. why price policy reaches Polymed through some channels and not others.

United States: group purchasing concentrates the buying

In the US, buying is concentrated in group purchasing organizations and hospital networks. A GPO aggregates the purchasing volume of its members and uses it "to negotiate discounts with manufacturers, distributors and other vendors". The GPOs' trade body counts 100+ national, regional and local GPOs used by more than 7,000 hospitals, and claims $55bn of savings a year, an advocacy figure.

The listed incumbents describe what this does to price:

  • BD says GPOs and integrated health delivery networks "concentrate purchasing decisions", which "has led to downward pricing pressure", that consolidating health systems add buying power and that "traditional distributors are also manufacturers" and so compete with it. Price contributed -0.3% to BD's FY25 revenue growth.
  • ICU Medical says large rivals win "full-line contracts" to supply all of a hospital's or GPO's infusion needs, and that a GPO contract "is no assurance that the sales volume ... will be maintained" because members may still buy elsewhere on price or quality. Most of its sales run under long-term contracts with prices "fixed for a set period of time", which is why it could not pass US tariffs on. One distributor accounted for 18% of its revenue.
  • Distribution runs through acute-care, non-acute, laboratory and wholesale distributors; Cardinal Health and Medline warehouse and ship a large share of Baxter's products. Both also sell their own-brand products (Section B2).

Polymed's route matches this structure. The MD described the market in 2023 as dominated by BD, B. Braun, Smiths Medical and Cardinal Health, with GPOs and distributors such as McKesson, Medline, PSS and Henry Schein, and noted that some GPOs serve large hospitals and others only day-surgery centres. Polymed has since signed contracts with two large GPOs and distributors, which "will be placing the product directly into the market", so that "our job is limited to manufacturing in India".

We read the US as a market that pays the highest prices but rewards breadth of range and price stability over the life of a contract. Under fixed-price contracts a tariff lands on the supplier, not the hospital, which is why the tariff path in Section B4 matters more to the economics of a US contract than its headline price.

Europe: public tenders, distributors and payback

European public hospitals buy through national and regional tenders. EU procurement allows a contract to be awarded on price alone or on the best price-quality ratio (the 'most economically advantageous tender', or MEAT, in EU usage), and the EU's own procurement instrument against Chinese bidders is designed around both kinds of award. Polymed's MD said in Feb-2023 that European and US buyers give quality and performance 70% of the weight and price the remainder: "if you fail the first two criteria, price is never a criteria for them".

Three features of European buying matter for Polymed:

  • The distributor is the customer. Outside Italy, Polymed sells through distributors, which normally hold 4-5 months of inventory to keep supplying national systems; the FY26 destocking showed how quickly that buffer can be run down (Section A3). Management has added its own clinical team to support distributors at hospital level.
  • Approval comes before the bid. The MD's summary: "CE mark doesn't mean anything unless and until you have approvals in local market ... and then you bid." In orthopaedics, Citieffe's management adds that many public tenders accept only bidders with a full portfolio. The MD said in Feb-2026 that the UK's NHS had delayed almost every contract by 1-1.5 years after the change of government.
  • Italy's payback. Under a 2015 law, device suppliers to the Italian national health system must repay part of any spending above regional ceilings. The Constitutional Court upheld the law in Jul-2024, and an Economy Decree of Jun-2025 let companies that dropped their appeals settle the 2015-2018 claims at 25% of the invoiced amounts. BD booked $62mn of payback accruals in FY24. Italian public spending on devices and services is about €10bn, per the industry association Confindustria Dispositivi Medici (2025). This matters to Plan1Health and Citieffe, which sell into Italian public hospitals, and to Italy as Polymed's only direct European market.

National and regional tenders, volume-based procurement and payback provisions all appear in Teleflex's list of pricing risks. Since 30-Jun-2025, under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1197, the EU has also excluded Chinese bidders from device tenders of €5mn and above (Section B4).

Emerging markets: the distributor holds the registration

In most of Latin America, Africa, West Asia and Asia a regional distributor or merchant exporter holds the product registration and the permission to sell. Replacing one is "operationally complex and time-consuming", which makes distributors sticky in both directions. Polymed sold through 260 distributors outside India in 1QFY25, "with many of them benefiting from local/regional exclusivity arrangements".

Two markets show how the registration shapes the route to market:

  • Brazil requires a Brazilian legal entity to hold the ANVISA registration. Polymed's distributors there "only sell our existing products"; for new ranges it will sell direct, and it bought Medyneo, a dormant company holding ANVISA and import licences, which management says saves 18-24 months.
  • Saudi Arabia requires a marketing authorization held through a licensed local authorized representative.

Payment is the other constraint. Management linked its cash conversion cycle of about 140 days in Aug-2026 partly to hard currency that is "not available in time in many markets".

China: volume-based procurement sets the floor

China buys a growing share of hospital consumables through provincial alliances and national VBP rounds, which trade a guaranteed volume for a large price cut. China ran 78 VBP projects for consumables in 2025, covering syringes, IV cannulas, vacuum blood-collection tubes and infusion sets among others. The first national round, for coronary stents, cut their price by 93%, to about RMB 700 per stent. An EU investigation found that 87% of Chinese public tenders for devices contain explicit or implicit bars on imported products.

Polymed barely sells in China, so VBP matters to it only indirectly: in Sanxin's words, the winners use the capacity VBP builds "to attack overseas markets", and we infer that Polymed's markets are among them (Section B2).

India: three channels with three price mechanisms

India's disposables reach patients through three channels that price in different ways.

  1. The trade channel. Distributors and dealers sell to private hospitals and nursing homes.
    • Polymed moved in 2022 from one distributor per state to several, some dedicated to a single hospital, with separate specialist distributors for dialysis chains, diagnostics and blood banks.
    • Prices differ by hospital, and distributors adjust them for payment terms: the MD said in Feb-2022 that good hospitals pay in three to four months and poor payers in six to nine.
    • Orders arrive case by case, not under long-term contracts.
  2. Corporate chains and organized providers. Large chains negotiate centrally.
    • Polymed introduced a single corporate-hospital price list with volume discounts from 1-Apr-2022.
    • It names Apollo, Max, Fortis, Manipal and Aster DM among its chain customers, and NephroPlus, DCDC and Apex among its dialysis chains.
    • The MD says Polymed is "present in almost every corporate hospital in the country", but in Feb-2025 he said it had only covered one-third of India's hospitals, with a share of wallet below 20% in those it serves; in Nov-2025 he put that share at 5-7%, calling it an estimate.
    • Organized dialysis chains buy centrally to get "cost-effective dialysis equipment and consumables".
  3. Government. Central and state tenders, state medical corporations and the Government e-Marketplace (GeM), where manufacturers usually bid through distributors.
    • Tenders are "subject to cancellations, re-bids and stringent qualification criteria".
    • The MD says they are won mostly on the lowest price, with "no significant quality advantage", and that many state governments take more than a year to pay.
    • Public procurement reserves syringes, needles, cannulas and urine catheters for local suppliers (Section B3).
    • Dialysis under the national programme (PMNDP) is bought as a service: the private operator supplies machines, dialysers and consumables. According to Frost & Sullivan's report in Nephrocare's Dec-2025 prospectus, the initial contract runs five years, extendable by five, at a price set by competitive bidding with a 3% annual escalation, and PM-JAY pays Rs. 1,650 per session on average.

Polymed has deliberately shrunk its government business, which management says earns lower prices and pays late. Government sales were about 20% of domestic revenue in mid-2024 and ~10-12% by 3QFY26, and they have fallen in every quarter management has commented on while private sales grew by 22.3-25% yoy.

Who pays the MRP, and why the trade margin matters

Every device sold in India carries a maximum retail price (MRP) printed by the manufacturer. The MRP matters less than it appears, because of who pays it:

  • Package rates. Under insurance and PM-JAY, the MD explained in 2022, "the whole package rate comes and then MRP doesn't matter". The MRP applies when a patient pays cash or is billed item by item. He estimated that MRP-based billing had fallen from 75% of hospital payments to 50% over five years and expected it to fall further as insurance spread; by May-2026 he put insurance at 60-65% of hospital payments.
  • The MRP is sticky. Under Para 20 of DPCO 2013 the MRP of a non-scheduled device may rise by at most 10% in any twelve months, so a brand launched at a low MRP cannot catch up with rivals that launched high. The MD's example was a competitor with twice Polymed's MRP, a level Polymed "cannot jump" to under the cap.
  • The trade margin is the gap. The gap between the landing price and the MRP is the trade margin. The drug-price regulator (NPPA) capped it at 70% of the price to distributor for oxygen concentrators by a notification of 3-Jun-2021 and for five more devices by one of 13-Jul-2021. The MD argued then that such a cap "does not impact the manufacturers it is only the trade margins".

The gap can be very wide. In a Sep-2026 survey by Maharashtra's drug regulator, as reported in the press, a Polymed IV set procured for Rs. 10.5 carried an MRP of Rs. 187, 17.8x the procurement price (our calculation). That was the lowest MRP and the lowest mark-up of the three IV sets named in the report (Section B3). The report does not say who bought at that price; it describes the gap as one between "trade procurement costs" and MRPs.

We draw three conclusions:

  1. Polymed's price sits near the trade procurement price, not the MRP. Its infusion price points of Rs. 10-20 per device are close to the procurement price the survey found, so we infer that most of the spread accrues to distributors and hospitals rather than to Polymed.
  2. A cap measured from the landing price would compress MRPs and channel margins first. The second-round risk is that hospitals and distributors, having lost margin, push back on purchase prices; a low-MRP brand could also lose less of its appeal to the channel than a high-MRP one. We cannot size either effect, because Polymed does not disclose how much of its domestic revenue is billed to patients at MRP.
  3. The package-rate shift works the same way over time. As more treatment is paid for as a package, hospitals gain from buying cheaper consumables, which favours makers with a cost edge.

What keeps a customer, and what does not

For hospital consumables the key buying criteria are product quality, surgeon preference and cost, and the decision-makers are "healthcare professionals, payers and hospital administrators".

Four things make a won account sticky:

  1. Contract terms. GPO contracts are multi-year, PMNDP contracts run five years or more, and Indian hospital prices are "announced for one year".
  2. Registrations held by the channel. A distributor that owns the registration is hard to replace, and so is the maker whose product it has registered.
  3. Equipment-linked consumables. Dialysis machines are placed against consumable contracts (Section A4.3).
  4. Training. Nurses and clinicians are trained on a device. Polymed runs 4,000+ customer-engagement programmes a year with 60+ clinical experts, and says its Indian programmes reached 80,000+ healthcare professionals in FY26. In its FY25 return under India's code for marketing practices in medical devices (UCMPMD 2024), it reported free samples worth between Rs. 420,565 (May-2024) and Rs. 1.8mn (Sep-2024) a month, against domestic sales of Rs. 4.9bn.

The evidence of stickiness is in Polymed's own record: management said 95%+ of export growth in 2QFY23 came from existing clients, and the top five customers were about 20-25% of revenue in Feb-2023.

Stickiness has limits. In commodity lines and public tenders price decides, a GPO contract does not guarantee volume, and Chinese makers offer prices well below Polymed's (Section B2).

How prices move

Prices of disposables move through six mechanisms. Section A4.1 sets out Polymed's own infusion price points and discounts to BD and B. Braun.

We see pricing in disposables as a slow ratchet: small annual increases, passed on only partly and with a lag, and bounded by tenders, reimbursement and cheaper imports. For Polymed the direction of travel is set less by its list prices than by its channel mix. The more it sells to private chains and export distributors on negotiated terms, and the less through lowest-price tenders and MRP-led trade, the less exposed it is to India's price-policy debate (Section B3).

B2 The competitor universe

Polymed competes in three leagues at once:

  1. Global majors many times its size, which sell whole portfolios into US GPOs and European tenders and also make and sell in India.
  2. Chinese exporters with similar cost structures and larger scale, now redirecting volume from the US towards Polymed's markets.
  3. Indian makers, mostly smaller and focused on one or two segments, several of them newly funded by private equity.

Section A8 compares margins and Polymed's competitive position. This section maps who the competitors are, what they make and where they meet Polymed, and the business-line chapters (A4.1-A4.10) go deeper by product.

How the field is structured

Three reports commissioned for Indian offer documents describe the same structure from different angles:

  • Three kinds of player. Frost & Sullivan (F&S, 2021) splits the Indian market into multinationals at the premium end, small domestic makers selling on price with variable quality, and a handful of "independent medical device companies" gaining share with multinational-grade quality at lower prices. Multinationals and independents together held 70-80% of the market.
  • Two layers. 1Lattice (2025) describes a commodity layer (syringes, IV sets, gloves, gowns), where domestic makers compete on price, scale and reach into smaller cities, and a premium layer, where multinationals and a few certified domestic firms compete on technology, international approvals and relationships with tertiary hospitals.
  • Few scaled Indian companies. F&S (2025) says the Indian MedTech industry "has very few scaled companies, such as PolyMed, SMT and Healthium". CRISIL (2024) counts more than 800 domestic device makers and describes the consumables market as "largely dominated together by MNC players and imports".

The offer documents also show how peers see Polymed:

  • G Surgiwear uses Polymed as its only listed peer, and Integris and SMT name Polymed and Laxmi Dental.
  • F&S classifies Polymed as an "Infusion, Vascular Access" company with 1 acquisition to Mar-2025 and Class I and II products only, and says "Polymed is most focused on consumables".

Global majors: bigger, broader and present in India

Four points stand out:

  1. Scale and breadth. BD's medication-delivery business alone is ~22x Polymed's revenue (our calculation), and ICU Medical says its rivals win "full-line contracts" because they can supply a hospital's whole infusion range. Breadth is the majors' main weapon in US GPOs and European tenders (Section B1).
  2. They are also in India. BD, B. Braun, Nipro and Terumo (through Terumo Penpol) make products in India. On CRISIL's FY23 figures BD India had revenue of Rs. 13.0bn and B. Braun India Rs. 6.1bn, with export shares of 15.9% and 23.1%.
  3. They raise prices where they can. Terumo's price increases more than offset its US tariff costs in the year to Mar-2026, and B. Braun, Nipro and Baxter also raised prices (Section B1).
  4. They are reshaping their portfolios. Teleflex is selling its acute-care and OEM businesses, Baxter sold its kidney-care arm to Carlyle, and BD bought Edwards' critical-care business (Section B5).

The distributors are a special case. BD notes that "traditional distributors are also manufacturers of medical devices, providing another source of competition". Medline and Cardinal Health sell own-brand products alongside the brands they distribute, and both were caught up in the FDA's 2023-2024 action against China-made syringes: Medline received a warning letter, and Cardinal's Monoject syringes, made by Jiangsu Caina, were recalled.

Chinese makers: scale at home, pressure abroad

The Chinese makers matter to Polymed because three forces now push their product out of China and away from the US:

  1. Price cuts at home. China ran 78 volume-based procurement projects for consumables in 2025, and KDL expects the new rules to concentrate the market in the leaders. Weigao says lower selling prices for certain core products under centralized procurement cut its device operating profit in 2025, and its gross margin was 46.3% in 1H26.
  2. Capacity built to win tenders. Sanxin says the winners of dialysis procurement rounds use the capacity those wins build "to attack overseas markets", where dialysis rates are rising in Southeast Asia and Latin America. Its overseas revenue rose 34.6% in 2025.
  3. A narrower US market. The FDA put Chinese syringe makers on import alert in 2024 and told US providers to avoid China-made syringes where possible, and the US raised its Section 301 tariff on Chinese syringes and needles to 100% from 27-Sep-2024 (Section B4).

The trade data show where the product went. China's device exports to the US fell 10.8% in 2025, while exports to the EU and UK rose 8.9% and those to Latin America 13.3%, both core Polymed markets. Weigao's US sales fell in 1H26 while its sales in Europe, West Asia and Africa rose.

The official data and management's account agree on direction but differ in degree: the MD's figures (in the note to Exhibit 88) imply a much larger swing than the industry data, which show growth of at most 13.3% in the regions reported outside the US. We use the industry data.

Indian makers: smaller, narrower, newly funded

We draw three points from the Indian field:

  • Few rivals match Polymed's breadth. Most Indian competitors are strong in one or two segments: HMD in syringes and needles, Healthium in sutures, SMT and Integris in stents, HLL and Terumo Penpol in blood bags. Romsons is the closest match on breadth and margin, and Polymed's placement document, citing CRISIL, puts it among the top five companies in India's device industry by operating income in FY23.
  • Rivals are adding capacity and claims. HMD claims capacity of more than 4.5 bn units per annum and describes itself as the world's largest maker of auto-disable syringes. Smaller makers such as Lars Medicare offer safety and closed IV catheters of the same generation as Polymed's.
  • Private capital is arriving. F&S (Oct-2025) counts about 59 MedTech private-equity deals in India since 2017. The recent ones:
    • KKR agreed in 2024 to buy Healthium from Apax in a deal valuing it at about $839.0mn;
    • ADIA invested $200.0mn in Meril in 2025, after Warburg Pincus's $210mn in 2022;
    • Kotak Alternate invested $48mn in Biorad Medisys;
    • Temasek completed a minority investment in Romsons on 22-Sep-2026, after reports in Oct-2025 of talks for 15-20% valuing the company at about $1bn. Romsons says it will look at acquisitions in India and abroad and a listing "at an appropriate time".
    • Healthium is buying a controlling stake in an advanced-surgery device maker, with a first tranche of about Rs. 6.0bn funded by debt.

Where the competitors meet Polymed, line by line

What the competitor map means for Polymed

We see Polymed's competitive position as strongest where it meets the Indian arms of the majors and single-segment Indian makers, and weakest where it meets Chinese exporters on price and the global majors on breadth:

  1. Against the majors, Polymed wins on cost and loses on range and brand. The MD put its prices at 15-20% below BD and B. Braun in infusion in 2023, which opens European tenders and Indian private hospitals but not, so far, US GPO volume.
  2. Against Chinese makers, it has no cost edge and sometimes a price disadvantage: the MD said in 2023 that Chinese dialysis products sold ~15% below Polymed's. Its defences are regulatory: the EU's exclusion of Chinese bidders from large tenders, US tariffs and FDA action against Chinese syringes, and the anti-dumping case it has brought in India (Sections B3 and B4).
  3. Against Indian makers, it has the widest range, the most export approvals and, by CRISIL's FY23 figures, the largest revenue among the Indian-owned disposables makers compared. The risk is that private capital narrows that lead, especially in syringes, cannulas and urology, where Romsons and HMD are strong.

B3 India medtech: market, policy and demand

India is Polymed's fastest-growing region and 31% of its FY26 revenue (Section A1). It is also where policy moves fastest, and in two directions at once. Industrial policy protects and subsidizes local makers through production incentives, local-content rules in public tenders and trade remedies. Price policy pushes the other way, through the cap on MRP increases, package rates for insured care and a live debate on capping trade margins. This section sets out the market, the policy on both sides and the demand drivers.

How big is the market? The estimates do not reconcile

No two sources size the Indian device market on the same basis. They differ on whether exports, capital equipment and diagnostics are included, on the year, and on who paid for the study. We show them side by side rather than choose one. Estimates from reports commissioned for offer documents or published by market-research firms are vendor estimates.

For Polymed the relevant pool is consumables and disposables, which the sources also size differently:

  • CRISIL puts consumables and disposables at Rs. 195.0bn in FY24, after 13% annual growth over FY19-FY24, and expects 11-12% a year to Rs. 290-300bn by FY28 (vendor estimate). It put Polymed's share at 1.9% in FY23, on domestic revenue of Rs. 3.4bn.
  • Frost & Sullivan puts disposables and consumables at $4.3bn in 2023, 26% of the device market, rising to $17.1bn by 2030 (vendor estimate).
  • 1Lattice puts surgical disposables alone at $3.9bn in FY25, rising to $6.4bn by FY30 (vendor estimate).

We use CRISIL's consumables figure as the working estimate of Polymed's domestic pool, because it is the only one that also measures Polymed's share. On that basis Polymed is a small player in a large market, and management frames the opportunity the same way: in Feb-2025 the MD said Polymed had only covered one-third of India's hospitals, with a share of wallet below 20% where it is present, and in Nov-2025 he put that share at 5-7%.

Imports, exports and the substitution runway

Import dependence is just as contested:

Two readings survive the noise. First, consumables are less import-dependent than equipment: BCG puts imported equipment at 60-65% in 2025 against 50-55% for consumables, CRISIL puts consumables at 30-40% against ~80% for all devices, and CRISIL says imports are lower in needles and syringes and higher in catheters and cannulas. Second, on BCG's estimates the import share is falling, and BCG expects domestic production to meet 75% of demand by 2035 (consultancy projection). CRISIL puts China at 16% of India's imports of medical and scientific instruments in FY24.

India is also a sizeable exporter, and consumables are its largest export category:

  • Exports were $4.0bn in FY25 by the Department of Pharmaceuticals' count, of which consumables and disposables $1.9bn. The export council's figures are close but not identical ($4.0bn and $1.8bn).
  • Apr-Feb FY26: exports were flat at $3.7bn, with exports to the US down to $670.39mn in the tariff period, while imports were $9.0bn, of which $1.4bn from China.
  • Net position. F&S, citing IBEF, says India became a net exporter of consumables and disposables in 2022-23, and the government says net device imports fell for the first time in 2023.

Policy, part one: rules that protect and support local makers

Licensing. All devices have been regulated under the Medical Devices Rules 2017 since Apr-2020, with licensing phased in from Oct-2022 (Class A and B) and Oct-2023 (Class C and D). Infusion sets are Class B and haemodialysers Class C. India had 4,108 licensed device manufacturers in Mar-2026. A draft amendment of Jun-2026 would make a notified-body audit of the quality system a condition of a licence and shorten review times. Management welcomed licensing as a way to push out unlicensed makers; in Aug-2022 the MD put the unregulated share of the industry at 70-75% before the rules took effect.

The draft devices law. The draft Drugs, Medical Devices and Cosmetics Bill 2026 has 190 sections and would replace the 1940 Act, add a technical advisory board for devices and extend criminal penalties for substandard or misbranded products to devices. A coalition of 11 industry associations led by AiMeD wrote to the Health Minister on 11-Aug-2026 asking for a separate Medical Devices Act and an autonomous regulator, and objecting to jail terms of 1-7 years. These details come from press reports; the official text was not available to us.

Production incentives (PLI). The scheme pays 5% of incremental sales over an FY20 base, subject to minimum sales growth. For Category A applicants the FY27 threshold is Rs. 2.8bn of incremental sales, and the incentive is capped at Rs. 1.2bn per applicant and target segment over FY23-FY27.

  • Polymed. It is approved for seven renal products (dialysers, dialysis machines, PD kits, fistula needles, bloodlines, haemodialysis catheters and transducer protectors) at Faridabad. The government lists the project as commissioned, with committed investment of Rs. 720mn and actual investment of Rs. 556mn. Polymed had received no incentive up to FY25: it is not among the recipients in the Jul-2026 parliamentary answer, and asked in May-2025 whether it had realized anything for renal, the MD said "No, Zero". He has said the scheme "has not worked well" because the thresholds are the same for equipment, implants and consumables. Whether anything was claimed for FY26 is [not disclosed].
  • Who has been paid. Incentives up to FY25 went to seven companies, including Nipro India Corporation, whose Satara plant makes dialysers, which received Rs. 349mn. The two official totals conflict: Rs. 2.7bn to FY25 in a Jul-2026 parliamentary answer, against Rs. 1.6bn to Dec-2025 in a Mar-2026 release.
  • A second scheme. Polymed also has a project under the scheme to reduce import dependence (MIS-RID) for polymer tubing, bloodline and central venous catheter components: project cost Rs. 1.0bn, grant Rs. 100mn.

Public procurement. Government buyers must prefer local suppliers. A Class-I local supplier needs at least 50% local content, and 19 device lines, including syringes, hollow needles, urine catheters, cannulas and blood-transfusion apparatus, are open only to Class-I suppliers whatever the tender value. Poly Medicure appears on the illustrative supplier list for these lines. Global tenders below a value threshold are barred unless a device is on an exemption list, which covered 364 devices to Mar-2024; our search of the published lists found none of Polymed's core products on it. Since Oct-2024 PLI makers count as Class-II suppliers; Nipro is listed for dialysers and Polymed is not.

Taxes and duties. GST on devices was cut from 12% to 5% on 22-Sep-2025, and management linked a one-off distributor destocking in 2QFY26 to the change (Section A3). Imports of medical instruments and equipment (HS 9018 to HS 9022) carry a health cess of 5% on top of basic duty. The duty structure is inverted: CRISIL notes GST of 5-18% across devices, and Polymed says inputs and job work attract higher GST and customs duty than finished devices, which favours importers in renal. From 2-Apr-2026 the government removed basic customs duty on a list of petrochemicals and polymers, including PP, PVC and polycarbonate, "in view of ongoing conflict in West Asia"; the relief lapsed after 15-Jul-2026.

The dialyser anti-dumping case

On 25-Jun-2026 the Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR) opened an anti-dumping investigation into disposable haemodialysis dialysers from China and Malaysia, on Polymed's petition. The case, the policy measure most directly aimed at Polymed's own problem, is set out below; Section A4.3 covers its effect on the renal business.

  • Scope. The period of investigation is calendar 2025, and the injury period also covers FY23-FY25. Certain Fresenius dialyser brands are excluded.
