  • Standing. Polymed told DGTR that it is "the major domestic producer"; the only other one is Nipro Medical India, a 100% export-oriented unit that makes dialysers almost entirely for export. DGTR accepted that Polymed constitutes the domestic industry.
  • Injury claimed. DGTR's initiation notice records prima facie evidence that dumped imports rose "significantly in absolute terms", undercut and depressed prices, and left the domestic industry with "financial losses, cash losses and negative return on capital employed" in the investigation period. Because Polymed alone constitutes the domestic industry in the case, we read this as a statement that its dialyser business made losses in the investigation period; the company does not report profitability by therapy line. Management says it claimed an injury margin of 20%.
  • Process. Questionnaire responses were due by 9-Sep-2026, and 11 parties have registered, including Weigao's blood-purification arm, Jiangxi Sanxin and a Malaysian exporter. No preliminary finding had been published by 24-Sep-2026. Management hopes for a decision "between now and end of the year".

Management says most Chinese makers ship to India at zero duty under the ASEAN free-trade agreement, and in May-2023 the MD described Chinese product being relabelled in Malaysia or Thailand and sent on to India duty-free. We read the trade data as consistent with that account: imports under the dialyser tariff line from Malaysia rose from $210k in FY23 to $13.74mn in FY26, and in units from 58,302 units to 6,060,880 units, while direct imports from China fell to 10,592,925 units in FY26 from 17,298,455 units a year earlier. The line also covers machines, so the data cannot prove the route.

Policy, part two: the price of a device and the trade-margin debate

Section B1 explains how the MRP and the trade margin work. Here we set out where the policy stands.

Today's rules. Non-scheduled devices, which include all of Polymed's consumables, face only the Para 20 limit: their MRP may rise by at most 10% in twelve months. Device prices have been set directly three times: ceiling prices on coronary stents and knee implants in 2017, and trade-margin caps on six devices in 2021, which the government says save consumers ~Rs. 10.0bn a year.

The Aug-Sep 2026 push. Three steps in six weeks turned trade margins on consumables into a live issue:

  1. Parliament, 7-Aug-2026. The standing committee on health recommended that "the gap should not be more than 20% between landing price and MRP for medical devices and drugs", and called for centralized, tender-based procurement of high-end devices and consumables by private empanelled hospitals.
  2. Maharashtra, 15-16 Sep 2026. The state drug regulator's price-monitoring unit surveyed inpatient consumables and found mark-ups of up to 2,841%, including on a Polymed IV set, and its commissioner asked the Department of Pharmaceuticals and NPPA to cap trade margins, issue guidelines on permissible price differentials and bring the items under DPCO. The drug regulators of Punjab, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu sent similar inputs.
  3. The Health Minister, 18-Sep-2026. After the department met private hospitals and FICCI on 17-Sep, J.P. Nadda directed it and NPPA to review the trade-margin exercises of 2004, 2008 and 2019 and to consult hospitals and industry. No public deadline has been set.

What NPPA can do. Trade press reports that NPPA has no blanket power to impose a single margin cap across non-scheduled devices; a broad cap would need an amendment to DPCO, or trade-margin rationalization category by category, the route taken for anti-cancer drugs in 2019 and for six devices in 2021. Non-scheduled products are 82% of the pharmaceutical market by value.

Who is on which side. The Association of Healthcare Providers, which represents around 30,000 private hospitals, argues that MRPs are "fixed upstream by manufacturers and distributors", that hospitals do not charge above MRP and that most treatment runs on insurance package rates. The domestic manufacturers' association (AiMeD) backs trade-margin caps based on ex-factory or landed import prices.

We see three outcomes, in rising order of impact on Polymed:

  1. No action, or monitoring only. The status quo, with the 10% limit on annual MRP increases.
  2. Trade-margin caps on named inpatient consumables (IV sets, syringes, catheters), as in 2021. MRPs of the affected products would fall towards a fixed mark-up over the price to distributor. On the 2021 precedent the cap applies to the channel, and the MD argued then that it "does not impact the manufacturers"; the risk to Polymed is a second-round push by hospitals and distributors for lower purchase prices.
  3. A general cap of 20% over landing price across devices, as the parliamentary committee proposed. That would require a DPCO amendment and would compress the channel's margin on every MRP-billed product.

In every case the exposure depends on how much of Polymed's domestic revenue is billed to patients at MRP rather than on package rates or institutional contracts, which the company does not disclose. We read the survey's single Polymed data point as a sign that it sets MRPs below rivals', not as proof.

Demand: what drives consumption

The demand story is well known; what matters for Polymed is how it is paid for. The shift from cash to insurance and government schemes moves hospitals from itemized MRP billing to fixed package rates, which rewards cheaper, reliable consumables; management says the shift, together with dearer imports, is pushing hospitals towards domestic products. Dialysis is the clearest case: the government pays a fixed rate per session, private operators run many public centres, and every session uses a dialyser, a bloodline set and a pair of fistula needles (Section A4.3).

We read India as Polymed's most attractive market on volume and its most uncertain on price. The volume case rests on insurance, PM-JAY and PMNDP; the price risk rests on a trade-margin decision for which no deadline has been set. We would watch the Department of Pharmaceuticals' assessment, the DGTR's preliminary findings on dialysers and any NPPA notification on inpatient consumables.

B4 Export-market regimes

Polymed earns ~69% of its revenue outside India, so the rules of its export markets matter as much as India's (Section A1). Three regimes set the terms: the EU's Medical Device Regulation (MDR) and procurement rules, which govern its largest export region; US clearance and tariff policy, which govern the largest market it barely serves; and a patchwork of registration rules, procurement systems and, since early 2026, war-related shipping costs in its other markets.

Europe: MDR, a procurement shield against China and a DEHP deadline

MDR. The MDR has applied since May-2021, and its certificates, issued by notified bodies, are valid for at most five years. It raised the cost and time of keeping each product on the market: management said in May-2022 that a CE mark now took 18-24 months, against six to twelve before, and in Feb-2026 that Polymed "had to drop many products initially". The EU has only 51 notified bodies designated under the MDR, for a medical-technology market the Commission puts at €170bn.

Polymed's position is strong: every plant is certified under the MDR for its full range, 89 products held MDR certificates in FY25, and management put its CE-certified range at ~75 products in Nov-2025, with ~20 more expected to be CE-marked in CY26; the two counts are on different bases, which the company does not reconcile (Appendix). The acquisitions also bought MDR-certified European manufacturing. The simplification proposal would lower costs for everyone and so narrow the advantage Polymed gained by paying the entry cost early (Section B5).

The procurement shield. The International Procurement Instrument measure is the EU's answer to China's closure of its own hospital market: an EU investigation found that 87% of Chinese public device tenders restrict imported products. Since 30-Jun-2025 Chinese bidders have been excluded from EU device tenders of €5mn or more, and winning bidders may source no more than 50% of the contract value from China. China responded by restricting European device makers in its own public procurement, per B. Braun.

We see the measure as a direct, if partial, benefit to Polymed. It removes Chinese makers from the largest European tenders just as Chinese pricing was hurting Polymed's European sales (Section A3), but it does not cover tenders below the threshold, private buyers or distributors' own sourcing, and the content cap still allows some Chinese components.

The UK. Management put the UK at about 5-6% of Polymed's revenue in FY25. Management says the India-UK trade agreement cuts UK import duty on most of its products from ~4-5% to near zero, and that NHS contracts were delayed by 1-1.5 years after the change of government.

United States: clearance, quality rules and a tariff path that keeps changing

Clearance and quality. Polymed's own FDA 510(k) clearances are all in infusion; its subsidiaries hold clearances for a pain-management catheter (Plan1Health), guiding catheters (PendraCare) and trauma implants (Citieffe) (Sections A4.1 and A8). The FDA's Quality Management System Regulation, which incorporates ISO 13485:2016, took effect on 2-Feb-2026, and management says the FDA now expects testing in US laboratories. The FDA has also turned against Chinese syringes: it advised US providers in 2024 to use syringes "not manufactured in China, if possible", and put several Chinese makers on import alert.

Tariffs. Medical instruments enter the US free of ordinary (MFN) duty, so every tariff Polymed has faced since 2025 has come from emergency or trade-remedy measures that were imposed, raised, struck down and replaced in quick succession.

Four points follow from the table:

  1. India's rate is back to where management can sell. The MD called the Aug-2025 rate of 50% "completely untenable" and said customers were waiting; by Aug-2026 he said "the duty is only 10%" and that the US pathway was still open.
  2. India now pays less than China on the products that matter. On syringes and needles China carries the 100% Section 301 duty; on all medical instruments the forced-labour action charges China 12.5% against India's 10%. The forced-labour action came only in Jul-2026, so we infer that it was the Section 301 duty on Chinese syringes and needles from Sep-2024, with the FDA's stance on Chinese syringes, that opened the US syringe market to Indian suppliers in 2025 (Section B5).
  3. Section 232 is the next risk for everyone. The Commerce Department opened a national-security investigation into imports of PPE, medical consumables and medical equipment on 2-Sep-2025. The statute gave Commerce 270 days from initiation to report to the President, a period that ended in late May-2026, and a finding could add tariffs on top of country rates whatever the origin. BD and ICU Medical both flag it as a risk; we found no published report or action as of 24-Sep-2026.
  4. India is also a target. A Section 301 investigation opened in Mar-2026 into excess capacity lists health among India's surplus sectors and cites a bilateral goods surplus of $42bn in 2025; no action has followed yet. In the Feb-2026 joint statement India agreed to "address long-standing barriers to the trade in U.S. medical devices".

For Polymed the direct exposure is small: management expects US exports of $3.5-4mn in FY27. The indirect effects are larger. US tariffs on China push Chinese product into Polymed's other markets (Section B2), and US tariffs on EU-made goods also apply to the European subsidiaries' US sales; B. Braun reported a 15% US tariff on EU-made medical technology in 2025, before the IEEPA duties were struck down.

Other markets: registration rules, tenders and war-risk freight

Freight. The Drewry World Container Index roughly doubled between April and September 2026, and the Shanghai-Rotterdam lane rose by about two-fifths. In September Drewry linked the latest rise to Transpacific demand ahead of China's Golden Week and carrier capacity management, and noted a gradual return of Suez services but renewed risk in the Red Sea; war-risk surcharges and insurance add to the cost of Gulf cargo. Polymed sells ex-factory in many markets, so customers bear much of the freight, but management says logistics costs have risen 2-3 times in six months and that longer delivery times have slowed collections.

Where India's cannula and catheter exports go. The trade data show why these regimes matter to Polymed. India's exports under HS 901839, the customs code for needles, catheters and cannulas, were $525.9mn in 2025 (our calculation from UN Comtrade). The largest buyers were the US, Brazil and the UAE, followed by Türkiye, Russia, Germany and France.

We draw two conclusions for Polymed. First, in the regimes that matter most Polymed has already paid the entry cost where it sells today: it holds MDR certificates for its range in Europe and US clearances for its safety catheters and IV sets, which makes these regimes barriers to others more than to Polymed in those products. Second, the risks are now mostly in trade policy and logistics rather than regulation: Section 232 in the US, the West Asia war, and whether the EU's shield against Chinese bidders holds.

B5 Structural trends

Nine structural trends will shape disposables over the rest of the decade. Most of them favour a low-cost maker that already has safety-engineered and PVC-free products, captive gamma sterilization and European and US approvals, which describes Polymed. Two cut the other way: Chinese makers redirecting volume from the US into Polymed's markets, and consolidation that gives rivals more scale and capital.

Safety-engineered devices

The EU's sharps directive (Directive 2010/32/EU), transposed by 11 May 2013, requires employers to provide devices with safety-engineered protection where a risk assessment calls for it, and bans recapping. CRISIL lists the safety devices now in use in India: safety IV cannulas and scalp-vein sets in infusion, safety blood-collection sets and fistula needles in dialysis, and safety Huber needles and closed IV catheter systems in critical care.

How far conversion has gone is uncertain. Two market-research vendors put the safety share of the IV-catheter market at 62% (Persistence, CY25) and 30.3% (Future Market Insights, CY26); both are vendor estimates, and neither splits the figure by region.

What it means for Polymed. Each hospital that converts moves from a conventional to a higher-priced safety cannula, and Polymed has FDA 510(k) clearances for its safety and closed IV catheters as well as EU approvals (Section A4.1). The share of its cannula volume that is already safety-engineered is [not disclosed], which is the number that would show how much conversion is left.

PVC and DEHP

DEHP is the plasticizer that makes PVC flexible in blood bags, bloodlines and infusion tubing. Under Regulation (EU) 2023/2482, its use in medical devices has a latest application date of 1 January 2029 and a sunset date of 1 July 2030, after which it needs an authorization. ICU Medical lists demand for "more environmentally friendly products" and "materials of concern" among the factors it competes on, and Fresenius introduced a PVC-free foil for its dialysate bags in 2025 and cut the material used in its bloodlines. HLL, which claims a dominant share of India's blood-bag market, sells PVC bags.

Polymed sold 965.3mn units of PVC-free products in FY25, 75% of the finished goods it sold, and aims to develop PVC-free versions for at least 15% of its portfolio by 2035. Its catalogue already includes blood bags with TOTM plasticizer for platelet storage, a DEHP- and PVC-free burette set, PVC-free extension lines and a DEHP-free Ryle's tube.

What it means for Polymed. We infer that the unit share is high because many of its products, such as cannulas, contain no PVC in the first place; the harder part is the PVC-based lines in blood management, renal and infusion tubing that it sells into Europe. We see the EU deadline as a moderate positive: it raises the cost of staying in the EU market for PVC-based rivals, but alternative plasticizers cost more and must be revalidated product by product.

Sterilization: ethylene oxide under pressure, gamma in-house

About 50% of sterile devices in the US are sterilized with ethylene oxide (EtO), per the FDA, which supports alternatives and treats radiation as an "established" method. The pressure on EtO is regulatory and legal:

  • the US EPA's emissions rule for sterilization facilities took effect on 5-Apr-2024 with two years to comply, and a presidential proclamation of Jul-2025 gave certain facilities two more years;
  • the EPA's interim registration decision of Jan-2025 tightens exposure limits, which BD warns could reduce sterilization capacity;
  • contract sterilizers have faced lawsuits.

Polymed commissioned a captive gamma-sterilization plant in 2025, which management expects to expand from 300 kci to 2,000 kci. Before it, sterilization was outsourced, and management called gamma a "more safer process compared to the ETO gas which we use today". Citieffe still outsources sterilization but plans to bring it in-house.

What it means for Polymed. Captive gamma shortens lead times, removes a dependence on third-party EtO capacity that tighter rules may shrink, and lowers cost at scale; management cites gamma savings among its offsets to raw-material inflation. The share of output that has moved to gamma, and what still needs EtO, is [not disclosed].

Closed systems and needle-free access

The leading infusion suppliers now sell the catheter as part of a system: BD's range includes flush syringes, disinfecting caps, needle-free connectors and closed-system transfer devices, and ICU Medical offers "a one-stop shop" of catheters, connectors, sets and pumps. CRISIL counts closed IV catheter systems among the safety devices in use in India.

What it means for Polymed. It has most of the parts: a closed IV catheter system cleared in the US (Nouvo), needle-free connectors, disinfecting caps and prefilled flush syringes. It lacks infusion pumps, which limits it in full-line US contracts (Section A4.1). We see this trend as raising the value per line for Polymed in Europe and India, where it sells without pumps, and as a barrier in the US.

Home dialysis and single-use dialysers

Estimates of how many patients dialyse at home depend on who counts:

  • Fresenius (worldwide, CY25): 89% of patients received haemodialysis in a clinic and 11% peritoneal dialysis (PD), mostly at home.
  • F&S (its study markets, 2024): PD below 5% of patients and home haemodialysis below 1%; it expects PD's share to stay minimal. In India, clinic haemodialysis is >98% of dialysis therapies.

Policy may push the other way in India. The parliamentary health committee's Aug-2026 report on kidney disease recommends promoting home-based PD and mandatory insurance for kidney patients. PM-JAY already pays a PD package of Rs. 1,500 for catheter insertion and Rs. 1,000 a day for fluid and disposables, and Assam's health mission funds PD at Rs. 15,000 per patient per month.

The other shift is to single use. Nipro expects Asian dialyser sales to grow on "the shift to single use", while Indian centres reuse dialysers several times (Section A4.3).

What it means for Polymed. Its renal range is built around haemodialysis: dialysers, bloodlines, fistula needles and machines, with PD kits among its PLI products. A move to home PD would shift demand towards PD fluids and kits, where Vantive and Fresenius lead; a move to single use would multiply dialyser volumes. We see single use as the larger and nearer effect for Polymed, and PD as a slow policy risk.

Automation and labour cost

F&S puts India's average hourly manufacturing wage below $2 per hour, against $5-6 per hour in China, $28-30 per hour in the US and $36-42 per hour in Europe, and India's manufacturing and R&D costs about 30% below those of the US and Europe.

Polymed pairs that labour-cost edge with automation: 530 automatic assembly machines and 130 robots in May-2026, against 200 assembly machines in Jun-2024. We read its workforce data as one reason: permanent-worker attrition was 74.6% in FY26, and 51.1% of permanent workers were paid the minimum wage. Chinese rivals are automating too: KDL reports pushing scale expansion, automation and intelligent upgrading at each of its four manufacturing bases.

What it means for Polymed. Against Western makers the labour gap is decisive; against China it is smaller, and against both it matters less as automation cuts labour content. We read Polymed's durable edge as automation plus in-house tooling and machine building (Section A8), with low wages as a diminishing bonus. Minimum-wage revisions and high attrition are the pressure points.

China+1, tariffs and supply security

US policy has pushed buyers away from Chinese syringes. The FDA advised providers in 2024 to use syringes "not manufactured in China, if possible", and the US raised its Section 301 tariff on Chinese syringes and needles to 100% from Sep-2024 (Section B4). US syringe imports show the result.

Other evidence points the same way, but slowly:

  • Buyers. 1Lattice reports that international buyers are turning to Indian suppliers for cost, flexible specifications and faster turnaround, and that "many companies are moving manufacturing from China to India".
  • Polymed. The MD said in Feb-2024 that "there is no shift from China today" for Polymed's products, and in Nov-2025 that US buyers had so far favoured Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia.
  • Chinese response. Chinese makers are localizing abroad: Weigao's Indonesian joint venture starts production in 2H26. China's drug regulator has also issued rules on export sales certificates, effective 1-May-2026, which KDL says will support device exports.
  • Supply security. Hurricane Helene's damage to a competitor's US IV-solutions plant in 2024 caused a national IV-fluid shortage, and B. Braun raised its inventory coverage to 19.8 weeks in 2025 "to ensure supply security". We would expect buyers that were short of product to be more willing to qualify a second source.

What it means for Polymed. China+1 is real in syringes and slow in cannulas. We see it as a multi-year opening in the US and with OEMs that source from Asia, which depends on US tariffs on India staying below those on China (Section B4) and on Polymed winning GPO volume.

EU MDR and supplier attrition

The MDR raised the cost of staying in Europe. F&S says it adds complexity, delays launches and raises entry barriers, and that Europe's funding squeeze favours overseas makers with a cost advantage. The EU now has 51 notified bodies designated under the MDR, and legacy certificates run out on 31 December 2027 for higher-risk devices and 31 December 2028 for the rest.

Attrition is visible in the evidence:

  • Polymed "had to drop many products initially" during the transition, and management said in May-2022 that a CE mark now took 18-24 months.
  • Translumina's German unit had its CE certificate suspended by its notified body for five months from Oct-2024.

Polymed has paid the entry cost: all its plants are certified under the MDR for their full range, and it had ~75 CE-certified products in Nov-2025, with ~20 more expected to be CE-marked in CY26. The Dec-2025 proposal to simplify the MDR would remove the five-year limit on certificates and, by the Commission's estimate, save >€3bn a year (Section B4).

What it means for Polymed. We read the MDR as having thinned the field of small suppliers in European tenders, and the acquisitions of PendraCare and Citieffe bought MDR-certified European manufacturing. The simplification lowers costs for all incumbents, including smaller rivals, so we see the moat widening less from here than it did in 2021-2025.

Consolidation and M&A

Two patterns stand out. The US majors are selling low-growth consumables and contract-manufacturing units (Teleflex's acute care and OEM businesses, Baxter's kidney care) to specialists and private equity, while buying higher-growth technology (BD's critical care, Teleflex's vascular intervention). In India, F&S counts 59 MedTech private-equity deals since 2017, and the latest have funded Polymed's closest domestic rivals.

What it means for Polymed. The carve-outs create owners of consumables lines who are under pressure to cut costs, and Teleflex's OEM unit, which makes catheters, extrusions and introducers for other device makers, shows that OEM supply is a business in its own right; CRISIL notes that OEMs have been seeking cost-competitive sources since Covid. That supports Polymed's contract-manufacturing push (Section A4.10). The offset is that its Indian rivals now have capital for capacity, acquisitions and exports.

Part C – Everything else

C1 Risk register

The register ranks the company-specific and industry risks that could change the business case we describe in Parts A and B.

  • Assessments. Likelihood and impact are our qualitative view, not forecasts.
  • Evidence. The evidence column shows what has already happened.
  • Monitoring. The monitor column points to where each risk would show up first; Section C2 turns those signals into a quarterly dashboard.

The three risks we weigh most

  1. Chinese pricing, in infusion and in renal. This is the risk most likely to change the margin structure.
    • In infusion, management credits new customers for the 1QFY27 European recovery (17.6% organic growth), which we read as evidence that the FY26 dip was largely cyclical.
    • In renal, the company has chosen price over volume; we see renal revenue growth as dependent on the outcome of the anti-dumping case.
  2. Execution on two acquisitions and three plants at once. The management layer is being built while integration and construction run in parallel. The early numbers for PendraCare are weak.
  3. Indian pricing policy. A cap on trade margins would compress MRP-based pricing in the domestic trade channel. Its effect depends on the channel mix, which Polymed does not disclose (Section B3).

C2 Quarterly monitoring dashboard

Each KPI below tests a driver from Section A7 or a risk from Section C1. The latest datapoint is the most recent disclosed figure; the "signal" column states what would change our reading of the business. Most items come from the quarterly presentation and call. Related-party, workforce and subsidiary data come once a year, with the annual report and BRSR in August.

Events to track outside the quarterly cycle:

  • DGTR's findings in the dialyser anti-dumping case;
  • the government's decision on trade margins for medical devices;
  • the US Section 232 outcome;
  • EU MDR certificate grants;
  • commissioning of the Palwal plant (Phase-1 targeted for Mar-2027) and the YEIDA plant (1QFY28 target);
  • changes in the promoter-group composition in the quarterly shareholding pattern.

C3 Plant-visit question bank

This chapter turns the open issues in this report into questions for a meeting with management during a plant visit. Each question card gives:

  • why the question matters, meaning the driver or disclosure gap it tests;
  • one line of context from our research;
  • what a reassuring or a concerning answer sounds like;
  • a follow-up.

It has three layers:

  • The must-ask list (below) is for a short meeting of about an hour.
  • The full bank is for a day-long visit with time for business-line heads, grouped by theme in the same order as the report.
  • The floor-walk checklist at the end lists things to observe rather than ask.

Compliance: ask about structure, not the current quarter

Listed-company managements cannot share unpublished price-sensitive information (UPSI) under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015.

  • What the questions do. They ask about business structure, strategy, economics and data the company has already disclosed.
  • What they avoid. Current-quarter trading, order-book numbers, unannounced transactions and changes to guidance.
  • If an answer strays into UPSI, stop the line of questioning and note it.
  • Numbers in the context lines come from public filings, presentations and call transcripts cited in this report.

Strategy and Vision 2030

Q01Must-askStrategy

Vision 2030 targets 2x revenue by FY30. How much of that do you expect from today's portfolio and plants, how much from the three new plants, and how much from acquisitions not yet made?

Why it matters
Separates organic capability from dependence on M&A. The answer tests every growth driver in Section A7.
Our context
FY26 revenue was Rs. 18.8bn, of which organic growth was 5.4% (our calculation). FY27 guidance is Rs. 23-24bn including the acquired businesses.
Listen for
Reassuring: a bottom-up bridge by therapy and region with capacity and approvals behind it. Concerning: a top-down number that leans on unnamed acquisitions.
Follow-up
Which two therapy lines have to beat plan for the target to hold?

Q02If time permitsStrategy

In mid-2024 you said the focus would stay on the existing segments; within about a year you had bought into cardiology catheters and trauma implants. What changed in your view of where Polymed should play?

Why it matters
Tests the consistency of the capital-allocation framework behind the acquisitions (Section A9).
Our context
Management's stated criterion is technology and regulatory approvals in adjacencies, because organic development takes 3-5 years.
Listen for
Reassuring: a clear filter (disease burden, approvals, manufacturing transferability) that also explains the deals rejected. Concerning: opportunism, or "we saw a good price".
Follow-up
Which adjacency would you not enter, and why?

Q03If time permitsStrategy

Between a low-cost volume manufacturer and a branded therapy company, where do you want Polymed to sit in 2030, and what share of revenue should be own-brand?

Why it matters
Positioning determines pricing power, margins and channel strategy for every line.
Our context
CRISIL puts own-brand sales at 70% of revenue; management put the OEM/private-label share at 28% in FY22.
Listen for
Reassuring: a deliberate plan to grow branded share in higher-value lines while keeping OEM for scale. Concerning: no view, or a view that ignores CRISIL's point that India's low-cost image limits premiums.
Follow-up
In which product lines do you already command a price premium over Chinese makers?

Q04If time permitsStrategy

Which region carries the most weight in Vision 2030 – India, Europe, the US or the rest of the world – and why?

Why it matters
Regions differ sharply in pricing, regulation and working capital.
Our context
Company-stated FY20-FY26 CAGRs: India 21%, Europe 20%, rest of world 15%. US exports are only $3.5-4mn a year.
Listen for
Reassuring: specific channel and approval plans for the US and for direct European markets. Concerning: the US treated as upside without a route to market.
Follow-up
What would it take for the US to become a double-digit share of revenue?

Q05If time permitsStrategy

You are building direct sales in Italy, Brazil, the UK and the US. What mix of direct versus distributor sales do you want by 2030, and what does going direct do to margins and working capital?

Why it matters
Going direct raises gross margin but adds fixed cost and receivables, a trade-off not visible in guidance.
Our context
The group has 590 direct-sales representatives across India, the US, Italy and Mexico, and bought Medyneo for its Brazilian licences.
Listen for
Reassuring: country-by-country payback periods. Concerning: direct selling pursued for control without a cost plan.
Follow-up
Which distributor relationships would you have to unwind, and at what cost?

Q06If time permitsStrategy

How do you decide whether to develop a product in-house or buy it, and how will the plan to double R&D spend change that balance?

Why it matters
R&D intensity is low against global peers, and it sets how fast the product range can move up the value chain.
Our context
R&D was 1.6% of revenue in FY26; management plans to double R&D spend over three to four years; the pipeline has 100+ products.
Listen for
Reassuring: named platforms, clinical programmes and a view on which regulatory markets each targets. Concerning: launch counts without revenue targets.
Follow-up
What share of FY26 revenue came from products launched in the last three years?

The FY26 reset and the recovery

Q07Must-askFY26 reset

Looking back at FY26, how much of the export shortfall was distributor destocking and how much was lost share or lower prices – and how do you know?

Why it matters
Decides whether FY26 was a cycle or a change in the export franchise (Section A3).
Our context
Standalone revenue grew only 4% in FY26 against consolidated growth guidance of 20%. Management cited destocking, faster Suez transit, Chinese product diverted to Europe and MDR renewals.
Listen for
Reassuring: named customers who destocked and have since reordered at similar prices, plus a volume-versus-price split. Concerning: a generic reference to market conditions.
Follow-up
Did you lose any customer in FY26, and to whom?

Q08If time permitsFY26 reset

What do the new European customers you are adding look like – tender wins, distributor switches or OEM programmes – and on what contract lengths?

Why it matters
New-customer quality determines whether the European recovery is durable.
Our context
Europe grew 17.6% organically in 1QFY27; management said it was adding 5-6 new European customers from April 2026.
Listen for
Reassuring: multi-year contracts with minimum volumes. Concerning: spot orders at lower prices.
Follow-up
How do the prices on these new contracts compare with the customers who destocked?

Q09If time permitsFY26 reset

What did the EU MDR transition cost you in dropped products and delayed certificates, and how much of the range is still waiting for certification?

Why it matters
MDR is a gate for European revenue and a moat against smaller competitors (Section B4).
Our context
Polymed received MDR certification for 89 products in FY25 and expected 15 products more within six months as of Feb-2026.
Listen for
Reassuring: a certificate schedule by notified body with dates. Concerning: open-ended waits or products abandoned.
Follow-up
Which competitors dropped products under MDR, and did you pick up their customers?

Q10If time permitsFY26 reset

West Asia is 6-8% of revenue. How are you serving the region while logistics are disrupted, and does the business come back at the same prices once routes reopen?

Why it matters
A regional shock with a working-capital tail; it also bears on PendraCare's West Asia exposure.
Our context
West Asia revenue fell 32% in 1QFY27 with orders held at port; management expects growth of 20-25% once the situation normalizes.
Listen for
Reassuring: orders deferred rather than cancelled, and no receivable stress. Concerning: distributors in financial difficulty.
Follow-up
What share of PendraCare's revenue goes to West Asia?

Q11If time permitsFY26 reset

Freight costs rose sharply. How much of the increase came from rates, how much from mode (air versus sea) and how much from volume, and what is a normal freight-to-revenue ratio for Polymed?

Why it matters
Freight is a swing margin line for a company that exports about two-thirds of its output.
Our context
Standalone freight was Rs. 334mn in FY26, against Rs. 245mn in FY25 and Rs. 113mn in FY24.
Listen for
Reassuring: contract rates, and customers bearing freight under their incoterms. Concerning: air freight used to recover service levels.
Follow-up
What share of export sales is on CIF versus FOB terms?

Q12If time permitsFY26 reset

How has FY26 changed the way you set and communicate guidance?

Why it matters
Guidance credibility matters for how the market reads the FY27 and FY30 targets (Section A3).
Our context
The upper end of FY27 standalone revenue guidance moved from Rs. 19.5bn to Rs. 20.0bn while being described as maintained.
Listen for
Reassuring: explicit assumptions (FX, acquisitions, West Asia) and ranges. Concerning: guidance defended as unchanged when it has moved.
Follow-up
Which single assumption carries the most risk in FY27 guidance?

Infusion therapy

Q13Must-askInfusion

What share of your IV cannula volume is safety-engineered today in each region, and what price premium does a safety cannula carry over a conventional one?

Why it matters
The shift to safety cannulas is the main price and margin lever in the largest line (Section A4.1).
Our context
Polymed is the world's third-largest IV cannula maker, with about 11% global share and 600mn units a year. Vendor estimates of the safety share of the IV-catheter market range from 30.3% to 62%.
Listen for
Reassuring: rising safety mix with a stable premium, and passive designs that you own. Concerning: safety cannulas priced at parity to win tenders.
Follow-up
Which safety designs (passive or active) are growing fastest, and do you hold the patents?

Q14Must-askInfusion

Prefilled saline flush syringes were 10.2% of FY26 standalone turnover. Where do you sell them, what capacity and utilization does the syringe line run at, and how do US duties on Chinese syringes change the opportunity?

Why it matters
A large product family that management rarely discusses, and a possible beneficiary of US trade action against Chinese syringes (Sections A4.1 and B4).
Our context
Launched in Nov-2020; management claimed 25-30% of the Indian market in May-2022, and the BRSR implies about Rs. 1.7bn of FY26 revenue (our calculation).
Listen for
Reassuring: US and European contracts with committed volumes, and the capacity to add lines. Concerning: flush syringes sold mainly as price-led tender volume.
Follow-up
None of Polymed's FDA listings is a syringe: when will you file a US 510(k) for PolyFlush, and do you make barrels and plungers in-house?

Q15If time permitsInfusion

How have realized prices per cannula moved over the last three years in Europe and in India, and what share of volume is under multi-year contracts?

Why it matters
Price erosion on mature products is offset by volume and cost; the balance determines infusion margins.
Our context
Management gave Indian price points of Rs. 10-20 a unit for mass products; the placement document describes selling prices that fall over a product's life.
Listen for
Reassuring: annual price resets linked to raw-material indices. Concerning: repeated price cuts to hold share against China.
Follow-up
Where did you walk away from a tender on price in the last year?

Q16If time permitsInfusion

What stops the US from being a much larger market for your infusion range: FDA clearances, group purchasing organization (GPO) contracts, OEM agreements or tariffs?

Why it matters
The US is the largest infusion market, and Polymed barely participates (Sections A4.1 and A5).
Our context
US exports run at $3.5-4mn a year. The tariff on Indian devices fell from 50% in Aug-2025 to 10% in Aug-2026.
Listen for
Reassuring: named GPO or OEM discussions and a US regulatory plan. Concerning: waiting for tariffs to fall.
Follow-up
How many 510(k)s do you need to offer a full US infusion catalogue?

Q17If time permitsInfusion

Needle-free connectors, closed systems, stopcocks and disinfecting caps: are they sold as kits with cannulas, and do they carry better margins than the cannula itself?

Why it matters
Accessory attach rates are a mix lever inside infusion.
Our context
The domestic catalogue offers needle-free connectors, closed IV catheters and the Polyswab disinfecting cap alongside cannulas.
Listen for
Reassuring: hospital-level bundles with measurable attach rates. Concerning: accessories sold only on distributor demand.
Follow-up
Which accessory has grown fastest over the last two years?

Q18If time permitsInfusion

What is your cost per cannula against the leading Chinese producers, and where does the gap come from – automation, needle-making, sterilization or raw materials?

Why it matters
The cost position is the core of the moat in commodity infusion (Section A8).
Our context
Management says it has 530 automatic assembly machines and 130 robots; CRISIL attributes margins to lower labour costs and in-house tooling.
Listen for
Reassuring: a quantified cost advantage by process step. Concerning: parity on cost with an advantage only on quality or service.
Follow-up
How has the gap moved since Chinese makers faced higher US duties?

Q19If time permitsInfusion

What were IV cannula revenue and volumes in FY24, FY25 and FY26, and how do they split between conventional, safety, blood-control and closed-system catheters?

Why it matters
The cannula is the anchor product but has no regular disclosure; the mix drives price per unit (Section A4.1).
Our context
The MD put cannulas at 25%-30% of revenue in Jul-2024 and volumes at about 600mn units a year.
Listen for
Reassuring: a volume figure with a rising safety share. Concerning: conventional export volumes falling.
Follow-up
Which cannula family grew fastest in FY26?

Q20If time permitsInfusion

What is the basis for the 11% global IV catheter share and the third-place ranking – volume or value, which competitors and which year?

Why it matters
A share claim that cannot be sourced weakens the scale argument (Section A8).
Our context
600mn units a year at 11% implies a market of about 5.5bn units (our calculation), far above the 1.5bn units a year cited in a 2024 clinical-trial record.
Listen for
Reassuring: a named data source and a definition that includes or excludes China. Concerning: an internal estimate.
Follow-up
Who are the two makers ranked above you?

Q21If time permitsInfusion

Why do annual infusion revenue figures sit below the sum of the four quarters, and why does the BRSR's infusion share imply a larger business than the annual report's segment table?

Why it matters
Growth rates and segment size depend on which classification is used (Sections A1 and A4.1).
Our context
The gap between the quarterly and annual infusion figures was Rs. 399mn in FY26; the BRSR implies Rs. 11.6bn against Rs. 10.0bn in the segment table (our calculations).
Listen for
Reassuring: a reconciliation and a stable definition. Concerning: products moved between segments without disclosure.
Follow-up
Which products sit in infusion in the BRSR but in "others" in the presentations?

Q22If time permitsInfusion

What volumes and prices are the two US group purchasing organization contracts and the US distributor contract delivering, and how are they affected by the Section 301 duty?

Why it matters
US revenue has lagged targets since 2022 despite several clearances (Section A5).
Our context
Management said in Aug-2025 that it had signed contracts with two large GPOs and distributors; Indian goods have paid a 10% Section 301 duty since 24-Jul-2026.
Listen for
Reassuring: repeat orders at prices close to Europe's. Concerning: one-off stocking orders.
Follow-up
How many US hospitals now buy Polymed cannulas?

Q23If time permitsInfusion

What will the polymer-tubing project supported by the government's MIS-RID scheme make, when does it start, and which imports does it replace?

Why it matters
In-house tubing is a cost and supply-security lever for infusion, renal and vascular lines.
Our context
The project costs Rs. 1.0bn, with a grant of Rs. 100mn, according to a Lok Sabha answer.
Listen for
Reassuring: a start-up date and a quantified saving. Concerning: an unfunded plan.
Follow-up
What share of tubing is imported today?

Vascular access and oncology

Q24If time permitsVascular and oncology

Plan1 grew from €7.25mn in CY23 to €10.5mn in CY25. Which products drove it – ports, PICCs or midlines – and is capacity at Amaro now the constraint?

Why it matters
Plan1 is the group's European manufacturing base in oncology access and its only profitable acquisition so far (Section A4.2).
Our context
Plan1 made a net profit of €681k in CY25 with 31 employees on average.
Listen for
Reassuring: growth across ports and PICCs with European tender wins. Concerning: growth driven by intra-group sales.
Follow-up
How much Plan1 product is sold through Polymed's distributors outside Italy?

Q25If time permitsVascular and oncology

Which Plan1 products are being industrialized in India, and how long does re-registration take under EU MDR and FDA for a new manufacturing site?

Why it matters
Transferring products to Indian plants lowers cost but carries regulatory friction.
Our context
Management plans to use Plan1 as the group's European base while shifting cost-sensitive production to India.
Listen for
Reassuring: a product-by-product transfer schedule. Concerning: no transfers yet planned.
Follow-up
Which Plan1 products have FDA clearance today?

Q26If time permitsVascular and oncology

What revenue ambition do you have for oncology access by 2030, and do you need another acquisition to get there?

Why it matters
Oncology is named in Vision 2030 but has no revenue target.
Our context
Revenue for the line is [not disclosed]; Plan1 is the only disclosed oncology business.
Listen for
Reassuring: a range built around ports and PICCs with clinical data. Concerning: a vague ambition.
Follow-up
Who are the two competitors you meet most often in port tenders?

Q27If time permitsVascular and oncology

Plan1Health's EBITDA margin has been described by management as 16-17%, but the company's slide shows 10.9% for CY24 and 13.4% for CY25. Which definition is right?

Why it matters
Plan1Health's record is used to justify the approach taken with later acquisitions (Section A4.2).
Our context
Management gave the higher figure on the 2QFY26 call.
Listen for
Reassuring: a reconciliation (for example before group charges). Concerning: no answer.
Follow-up
What margin do you target for Plan1Health by FY30?

Q28If time permitsVascular and oncology

Does Plan1Health carry any accrual for Italy's medical-device payback scheme, and what share of its sales goes to Italian public hospitals?

Why it matters
The payback can claw back part of past sales to Italian public hospitals; Plan1Health sells directly in Italy.
Our context
BD booked $62mn for the Italian payback in its FY24 accounts.
Listen for
Reassuring: a quantified provision or a clear reason none is needed. Concerning: no assessment.
Follow-up
Does Citieffe face the same exposure?

Q29If time permitsVascular and oncology

Who is the large Class III OEM customer that Plan1Health supplies, and what share of Plan1Health's revenue does it represent?

Why it matters
Single-customer concentration inside a subsidiary.
Our context
Management describes Plan1Health as the sole approved supplier to a large OEM.
Listen for
Reassuring: a multi-year contract. Concerning: an annual purchase order.
Follow-up
Does the OEM have a second source?

Renal care

Q30Must-askRenal

Management says Chinese dialysers enter India duty-free, paying 5% GST, while Polymed pays customs duty of 2.5% on imported raw materials and 18% GST. What is the landed price gap per dialyser today, and what happens to renal pricing if the anti-dumping investigation into dialysers from China and Malaysia does not lead to duties?

Why it matters
Dialyser pricing sets renal margins and the payback on the PLI-backed capacity (Section A4.3).
Our context
Polymed filed the petition (initiated 25-Jun-2026) and claims an injury margin of 20%. It told DGTR that the domestic industry made financial and cash losses and a negative return on capital in CY25. Renal revenue grew -3.8% yoy in 1QFY27 as Polymed chose price over volume.
Listen for
Reassuring: cost-down plans that close the gap without duties. Concerning: a strategy that depends on the trade remedy.
Follow-up
What duty would restore dialyser profitability, and how large were the losses the petition describes?

Q31Must-askRenal

What is the annual consumables pull-through per installed dialysis machine – bloodlines, fistula needles and dialysers – and what share of machines is sold outright versus placed against consumable commitments?

Why it matters
The razor-and-blade logic is the case for the machine business; placement terms decide its capital intensity.
Our context
Polymed placed 450 machines in FY26 against 500-600 guided, taking the installed base to about 1,000 machines. It had bid for 600 machines by Feb-2026.
Listen for
Reassuring: contractual consumable commitments and measured pull-through per machine. Concerning: machines sold at low margins without consumable lock-in.
Follow-up
How many service engineers support the installed base, and what uptime do you commit to?

Q32If time permitsRenal

Management said the single-use share of dialysers moved to 30-35% of the market and could reach 50% single use and 50% multi-use. What drives conversion – PMNDP rules, private chains or infection data – and what does it do to your volumes?

Why it matters
Each point of single-use conversion multiplies dialyser volumes, because a reused dialyser serves several sessions.
Our context
Management said reuse was the norm a few years earlier, with each dialyser reused 6x-8x (May-2023).
Listen for
Reassuring: named policy or chain decisions behind the shift. Concerning: conversion assumed rather than observed.
Follow-up
What price difference makes a centre switch from reuse to single use?

Q33If time permitsRenal

Your dialyser market share target moves from 10-12% to 15-17% and to 20-25% by 2030. Which customer groups get you there: PMNDP operators, dialysis chains or hospitals?

Why it matters
The customer groups differ in price, payment terms and switching costs.
Our context
PMNDP operates in 751 districts with 1,704 centres, according to the company.
Listen for
Reassuring: named chain contracts and PPP operators. Concerning: reliance on government tenders alone.
Follow-up
Are you on the approved list of the largest private dialysis chains?

Q34If time permitsRenal

Parliamentary data show no PLI incentive paid to Polymed so far, although it has invested Rs. 556mn of the Rs. 720mn it committed. Which thresholds have not been met, and what happens to the economics of the dialyser capacity if the incentive never comes?

Why it matters
The PLI's economics depend on hitting thresholds; the FY26 annual report discloses no PLI receipt (Section B3).
Our context
Management described an incremental-revenue requirement of Rs. 600mn a year. Nipro, the other domestic dialyser maker, received Rs. 349mn of PLI incentive over FY23-FY25.
Listen for
Reassuring: incentive accrued on track. Concerning: thresholds missed and incentive at risk.
Follow-up
What happens to the dialyser capacity if the PLI lapses?

Q35If time permitsRenal

Government reimbursement per dialysis session rose from ~Rs. 1,200 to Rs. 1,800 under the National Dialysis Programme and Ayushman Bharat, according to management. Does any of that reach consumable prices, and who sets the consumables price in PPP contracts?

Why it matters
Tests whether renal pricing has any link to reimbursement.
Our context
Management cited the change on the 3QFY25 call.
Listen for
Reassuring: contracts with operators that pass through part of the increase. Concerning: consumables priced purely on tender.
Follow-up
Who is the largest PPP dialysis operator you supply?

Q36If time permitsRenal

How much of the dialysis machine is made in India, and which modules are still imported?

Why it matters
Local content drives cost, lead times and eligibility for procurement preferences.
Our context
Management put local content at 50%.
Listen for
Reassuring: a plan to localize pumps and electronics. Concerning: dependence on one foreign module supplier.
Follow-up
What is the warranty cost per machine?

Q37If time permitsRenal

Do you have a plan for peritoneal dialysis or home haemodialysis, where the market is moving in developed countries?

Why it matters
Home dialysis is a structural trend that could bypass centre-based consumables (Section B5).
Our context
Polymed's range already includes peritoneal-dialysis sets; there is no disclosed home-dialysis programme.
Listen for
Reassuring: a considered position either way. Concerning: no view.
Follow-up
Which global player would you partner with in home dialysis?

Blood management and diagnostics

Q38If time permitsBlood and diagnostics

Blood management and blood collection is 9.5% of standalone turnover. How does that split between blood bags, collection tubes and needles, and who buys each?

Why it matters
The BRSR is the only disclosure of this line's size; the product split decides its growth and margin profile (Sections A4.4 and A4.5).
Our context
The BRSR share implies about Rs. 1.6bn of FY26 revenue (our calculation).
Listen for
Reassuring: growth in collection tubes and branded bags to private blood banks. Concerning: dependence on government blood-bank tenders.

What is your share of blood bags in India?

Q39If time permitsBlood and diagnostics

Where are you on DEHP-free blood bags, given the EU REACH sunset for DEHP in medical devices, and is there a price premium?

DEHP substitution is a regulatory transition that favours makers with validated alternatives (Section B5).

Polymed sold 965.3mn units of PVC-free products in FY25; DEHP's latest application date for medical devices in the EU is 1 January 2029.
Listen for
Reassuring: validated DEHP-free bags with European approvals. Concerning: no plan before the deadline.

Which plasticizer have you chosen, and who supplies it?

Q40If time permitsBlood and diagnostics

In vacuum blood-collection tubes, how do you compete with BD and Greiner in India, and is the line capacity-constrained?

Why it matters
Diagnostics is a high-volume line with global incumbents; the answer tests Polymed's right to win.

Revenue for tubes is [not disclosed]; they sit within the BRSR's blood-management line.
Listen for
Reassuring: private-lab contracts and a cost advantage. Concerning: presence only in low-end tenders.

Do you sell tubes and needles as a system to laboratories?

Anaesthesia, critical care, urology and surgery

Anaesthesia and respiratory was 2.9% of standalone turnover in FY25 but has no separate line in the FY26 BRSR. Where did it go, and what are your ambitions in critical care?

Reassuring: a reclassification explained, with revenue growth in critical care. Concerning: a shrinking line.

Urology (3.0% of standalone turnover) and surgery and wound drainage (5.3%) – are these branded products with hospital preference or tender commodities?

In enteral feeding and gastro products, what exposure do you have to the ENFit connector transition in export markets?

Reassuring: ENFit-compliant ranges ready. Concerning: legacy connectors in export ranges.

Q44If time permitsOther lines

What was critical-care revenue in FY26, did it grow the almost 2 and 1/2 times management hoped for, and how much of it overlaps with vascular access and infusion?

Reassuring: a revenue figure and the number of ICU accounts. Concerning: the target dropped without comment.

Q45If time permitsOther lines

How much do you sell in the US of Class I respiratory items such as suction catheters, circuits and masks, and how much of it is private label?

These items need no 510(k) and could scale faster than cleared products.

Your ambition is Rs. 3-4bn of cardiology revenue by 2030. What is the mix between stents, balloons, catheters and guidewires, and between India and exports?

Orthopaedics

Citieffe's revenue was flat in CY25, and its statutory accounts show a loss driven by FX. What EBITDA margin do you target, by when, and what are the three biggest cost levers?

Enterprise value €31mn, or 10.2x FY24 EBITDA; debt €13.1mn; plant utilization about 60%.

Q54If time permitsOrthopaedics

€3.38mn of Citieffe's receivables were more than 120 days overdue at end-CY25. Which countries are they in, and what is the collection plan?

Q55If time permitsOrthopaedics

Reassuring: focused trauma niches with surgeon relationships. Concerning: head-on competition with the majors.
Follow-up
What did the cancelled Latin American tender teach you about pricing?

Q56If time permitsOrthopaedics

How is Citieffe growing in calendar 2026 in euros, and has the cancelled Latin American tender been replaced?

Reassuring: a tender pipeline in Mexico and Latin America. Concerning: reliance on Italy.
Follow-up
Which US states is Citieffe entering?

Customers and channel

Q57Must-askCustomers and channel

What share of revenue is OEM or private label today, who are the largest OEM customers by product line, and what are the contract terms – tenor, exclusivity and price resets?

Why it matters
OEM supply gives volume but ties pricing to a few buyers; the split is not disclosed (Section A4.10).
Our context
Management put the OEM/private-label share at 28% in FY22; top-10 customers were 29.0% of FY24 revenue; no customer reached the 10% disclosure threshold in FY26.
Listen for
Reassuring: diversified OEM customers on multi-year contracts. Concerning: one or two global customers with annual price resets.
Follow-up
Are any OEM customers also competitors in your own-brand markets?

Q58If time permitsCustomers and channel

In India, how is revenue split between distributors, direct hospital accounts and government tenders, and how has that changed?

Why it matters
The channel mix drives exposure to the trade-margin debate and to government payment cycles (Section B1).
Our context
Private-sector revenue grew 25% in 1QFY26 while government business fell 10%.
Listen for
Reassuring: rate contracts with large chains and fewer, larger distributors. Concerning: dependence on a few super-distributors.
Follow-up
How many hospitals do you cover directly?

Q59If time permitsCustomers and channel

How many months of stock do your European distributors hold today, compared with before FY26?

Why it matters
Inventory in the channel was the main stated cause of the FY26 slowdown.

Listen for
Reassuring: data from distributor reporting. Concerning: estimates.
Follow-up
Do you have sell-out data from distributors?

Q60If time permitsCustomers and channel

What are payment terms by region, and how do you manage credit risk with distributors in emerging markets?

Why it matters

Our context

Listen for
Reassuring: credit insurance and letters of credit in higher-risk markets. Concerning: extended terms to win share.
Follow-up
What were bad-debt write-offs over the last three years?

Q61If time permitsCustomers and channel

Your OEM and CDMO pipeline: what did the two contract-manufacturing agreements signed in 1QFY26 cover, and how large could that business become?

Why it matters

Listen for
Reassuring: named product categories and customers' regulatory filings. Concerning: pilot projects without volume.

Q62If time permitsCustomers and channel

How do OEM and private-label margins compare with own-brand margins, and who are the largest OEM customers?

Reassuring: a narrow margin gap and diversified customers. Concerning: OEM priced near cost.

Q63If time permitsCustomers and channel

How large is the components business – catheters, guidewires, introducers, stopcocks and tubing sold to other device makers – and who buys from it?

Reassuring: a revenue range and repeat customers. Concerning: occasional sales.

Reassuring: a diversified country list. Concerning: dependence on a few distributors in two or three countries.

Reassuring: a country, a date and a payback plan. Concerning: an open-ended plan.

Q66If time permitsCustomers and channel

Listen for
Reassuring: product-level volumes from GPO contracts. Concerning: the target restated without a plan.

Q67If time permitsCustomers and channel

Which subsidiary booked the one-off provision of about Rs. 90mn in 4QFY26, and what was it for?

Why it matters
Management described it in different ways on the call (Section A5).

The provision hit 4QFY26 consolidated margins.
Listen for
Reassuring: a named, non-recurring item. Concerning: a recurring cost in an acquired business.

Competition

Q69Must-askCompetition

In European infusion tenders, what is the price gap to Chinese bidders today, and on which tenders do you win despite a higher price?

Why it matters
Identifies the non-price advantages – quality, delivery, MDR compliance – that protect share.
Our context
Management said Chinese product was redirected from the US to Europe in 1HFY26.
Listen for
Reassuring: tender criteria that reward quality (MEAT) and service. Concerning: winning only where you match Chinese prices.
Follow-up
How does the EU's International Procurement Instrument measure affect Chinese bidders in your tenders?

Q70If time permitsCompetition

Who is your toughest competitor in infusion, in renal and in blood management, and where have you lost share in the last two years?

Why it matters
A direct test of competitive position by line.
Our context
CRISIL names Baxter, BD, B. Braun, Boston Scientific and unorganized local players as competitors.
Listen for
Reassuring: specific names with reasons. Concerning: "no real competition".
Follow-up
What would a competitor need to do to take your largest account?

Q71If time permitsCompetition

Where do you overlap with Indian peers such as HMD, Romsons, Iscon and Healthium, and how do their prices compare?

Why it matters
Domestic competition sets prices in India's trade channel (Section B2).
Our context

Listen for
Reassuring: a quality and range advantage that holds a premium. Concerning: price-matching.
Follow-up
Which Indian peer is investing most in automation?

Q72If time permitsCompetition

Do global majors such as BD, B. Braun and Terumo buy from you as OEM customers, compete with you, or both?

Why it matters
A dual relationship affects negotiating power and disclosure.

Reassuring: a clear separation of OEM and own-brand markets. Concerning: OEM customers restricting your own-brand sales.
Follow-up
Has any major moved production away from you in the last three years?

Q73If time permitsCompetition

How do you see Chinese producers building plants in Southeast Asia to avoid US duties and Indian trade remedies?

Reassuring: a cost position that competes without trade protection. Concerning: dependence on remedies.

Q74If time permitsCompetition

Where do Romsons, Healthium and Hindustan Syringes compete most directly with Polymed, and has trade pricing in India changed since they raised private capital?

Our context

Reassuring: product-level differentiation and stable prices. Concerning: price cuts in cannulas, syringes or urology.

Q75If time permitsCompetition

Have US or European device makers moved syringe, cannula or component sourcing from China to Polymed since the FDA's syringe alerts and the Section 301 increases?

Why it matters

Our context
US syringe imports from India rose 16x in 2025 (our calculation), while imports from China fell; Polymed's FDA listings include no syringe.
Listen for
Reassuring: named OEM or CDMO programmes. Concerning: no inbound demand.
Follow-up

Industry, regulation and policy

Q76Must-askRegulation and policy

What share of domestic revenue is sold through the trade channel at MRP, what trade margin do your products typically carry today, and how would a cap on trade margins change your realizations?

Why it matters
India is weighing a cap on trade margins for medical devices; the exposure depends on the channel mix and MRP headroom (Section B3).
Our context
A press report of a Maharashtra FDA survey named a Polymed IV set bought at Rs. 10.5 against an MRP of Rs. 187, a mark-up of 1,681%. The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health recommended capping the gap between landing price and MRP at 20% in Aug-2026, and the Health Minister ordered a review. Domestic revenue was Rs. 5.8bn in FY26.
Listen for
Reassuring: modest trade margins and hospital-led pricing. Concerning: MRPs set well above realized prices.
Follow-up
What share of domestic revenue is billed to patients at MRP, as against package rates, chain contracts or tenders – and would you reset MRPs ahead of a cap?

Q77Must-askRegulation and policy

With the US tariff on Indian devices at 10% and higher US duties on Chinese syringes and needles, which of your products become competitive in the US, and what is your exposure to the Section 232 investigation?

Why it matters
US trade policy is the largest external swing factor for the export thesis (Section B4).
Our context
The duty on Indian HS 9018 goods rose to 25% plus a further 25% in Aug-2025, fell to nil after the Supreme Court's IEEPA ruling of 20-Feb-2026, and is now a 10% Section 301 duty from 24-Jul-2026. Chinese syringes and needles pay 100% under Section 301. US syringe imports from India (all makers) rose from $930k in 2024 to $14.8mn in 2025, while imports from China fell.
Listen for
Reassuring: product-by-product US plans. Concerning: US ambitions contingent on tariff outcomes.
Follow-up
Commerce had 270 days to report on Section 232. Are you considering US-side packaging, assembly or sourcing to qualify for any exemption?

Q78If time permitsRegulation and policy

How does the DPCO cap on annual price increases interact with your pass-through of raw-material costs in India?

Why it matters
Limits domestic pricing flexibility in inflationary periods.
Our context
The cap is 10% in any 12-month period for non-scheduled devices.
Listen for
Reassuring: annual price increases taken routinely. Concerning: price increases delayed or foregone.
Follow-up
Which products are closest to their price ceilings?

Q79If time permitsRegulation and policy

Which notified bodies certify your products under EU MDR, and how many certificates expire before the 2027-28 transition deadlines?

Why it matters
Certificate continuity is a gate for European revenue.
Our context

Listen for
Reassuring: all legacy certificates covered by applications. Concerning: products at risk of lapse.
Follow-up

Why it matters

Reassuring: recent clean inspections. Concerning: no inspection history at the plants that would supply the US.

Manufacturing, capacity and automation

Q94Must-askManufacturing

Why it matters
Utilization decides operating leverage and the timing of new capex (Section A6).

Installed capacity is 1.9bn units a year. Management put utilization at 65-70% in May-2026, against 75-80% in Jul-2024. The Aug-2024 placement document gave FY24 utilization of 70.5% in its chartered engineer's table but 80.7% in its management discussion.
Listen for
Reassuring: data by line with a clear bottleneck. Concerning: only a blended figure.

Reassuring: measured labour productivity by line. Concerning: automation counts without output metrics.

Q111Must-askQuality and sterilization

Polymed commissioned a gamma sterilization facility in 2025; management described a capacity path from 300 kci to 2,000 kci. PolyFlush syringes are gamma-sterilized.

Reassuring: in-house gamma lowering cost and cycle time. Concerning: dependence on third-party EtO sterilizers.

Which customer audit was the toughest, and why?

Other products

Regulatory approvals by market

Approvals decide where Polymed can sell, and they are slow to obtain. The company says its products are registered in 100+ countries and that it employs 200+ quality and regulatory professionals. Management said in May 2022 that a CE mark had come to take 18-24 months, and in May 2026 it put the time saved by buying a Brazilian company with licences in hand at 18-24 months. This appendix lists the approvals we could verify in regulator databases and company filings, market by market.

United States: 510(k) clearances

The MD calls the US "a very high price market". Devices that need FDA clearance reach it through the 510(k) route, in which the FDA finds a device substantially equivalent to one already on the market; every decision in the table below is of that kind. Polymed's own clearances are all infusion devices and all date from 2023 onwards; the older clearances came with Plan1Health, PendraCare and Citieffe.

What the list shows:

  • The count. The FDA database holds 22 510(k) records for the four applicants, 7 more than the 15 US approvals the company cites (our calculation).
  • Reconciling the two. The May-2026 deck splits the company's count into 4 for Polymed, 10 for Citieffe and 1 for Plan1Health, and says only that PendraCare's guiding catheter is approved. Polymed's and Citieffe's figures equal their Traditional submissions in the table, so we read the company's count as leaving out Special 510(k)s and PendraCare's clearances.
  • Recent additions. Since Apr 2025 the group has added the Primum guiding catheter, the Estremo fibular nail, Special 510(k)s for the Polyshield catheter and the Polywin Safety size range, and PendraCare's SimplGuide introducer.
  • A testing setback. In Nov 2025 the MD said the FDA had stopped accepting test results from Indian laboratories, so Polymed had to retest its products in the US: "all work we have done in the past was negated". The Aug-2026 deck still showed 11-13 US approvals in the pipeline.
  • The quality rule. From 2 Feb 2026 the FDA's device quality rule incorporates ISO 13485 by reference, the standard to which every Indian plant was certified at the Aug-2024 placement.

United States: establishment registration and device listing

The registration and listing records show which Polymed plants are registered with the FDA, which devices each is set up to ship to the US, and, through proprietary names, some of the private-label supply.

The records show:

  • A clean record. The database holds 19 listings under the Polymed name, and openFDA returned 0 recall or enforcement records for the company.
  • Private label. The suction catheter kit listed at Jaipur carries the proprietary name "McKesson", which the MD has named among the large US distributors and purchasing organizations; we read it as private-label supply.
  • Two clearances without a listing under the Polymed name. The Polyfusion IV sets (K220312) and the Nouvo Safety Set (K232234) do not appear in the listings retrieved under the Polymed name, while the listing for the Polyshield catheter cleared under K252677 was created on 10 Sep 2026. We could not tell whether the first two are listed under another firm's registration or not yet shipped, and we add the point to our questions.

European Union: MDR and CE marking

Europe produced 32% of FY26 revenue, and a device sold there needs a CE mark. Depending on its risk class, the maker must involve an independent notified body before it can affix the mark. When the Medical Device Regulation, EU Regulation 2017/745, took effect on 26 May 2021, the number of designated notified bodies was very low, which the European Commission says created bottlenecks in pre-market certification. Management said in Feb 2026 that Polymed "had to drop many products initially in the bargain because it was taking a long time to get the approvals".

The FY26 annual report does not name the notified body behind the MDR certificates. The company's EU product count has not moved in a straight line, and the counts are not on a consistent basis: "medical device products" certified in one deck, "approved" products in another and an approximate figure on a call. None of the disclosures says whether a product is a family, a code or a certificate.

The transition rules set the deadline for any directive-era certificates still in use:

  • Transition. Under EU Regulation 2023/607, devices certified under the old directives may stay on the market until 31 Dec 2027 for class III and implantable class IIb devices and until 31 Dec 2028 for other classes, provided the maker had applied for MDR certification by 26 May 2024 and signed with a notified body by 26 Sep 2024.
  • Revision. The Commission proposed a targeted revision of the MDR in Dec 2025, and the European Parliament's health committee began work on it on 14 Jul 2026.
  • The acquired makers. Citieffe says its whole portfolio is already certified under MDR, while PendraCare's products carry a mix of directive and MDR approvals; PendraCare's acquisition call described EU approvals as "extremely challenging" to obtain under MDR.

Plant quality certificates: ISO 13485, MDSAP and Korea GMP

ISO 13485 is the device quality-system standard that the FDA's quality rule incorporates from 2 Feb 2026. MDSAP certification covers Brazil, the US and Australia, and the MD said it "fast tracks our registration process".

Plant names follow the Aug-2024 placement document. The certificates for the FY26 facilities, the new Haridwar plant and the gamma sterilization facility, come from the FY26 annual report; Citieffe's plant certificates are not disclosed. By the company's count, ~70% of its facilities held ISO 14001 in Aug 2026.

Other markets

What to watch

Board and key management

At 31 Mar 2026 Polymed's board had 12 directors: 4 executive (our calculation) and 8 non-executive, of whom 5 were independent. The Aug-2024 placement document had shown 12 directors, 7 of them independent. The changes since then:

  • Independent terms ended. Dr Shailendra Raj Mehta and Dr Sandeep Bhargava left on completing their terms on 26 Sep 2024.
  • The chairman was reclassified. D.R. Mehta's tenure as an independent director ended at the 29th AGM in Sep 2024, and shareholders re-appointed him as a non-executive, non-independent director. The 31st AGM re-appointed him by special resolution, which is required because he is over 75 years old; 4.0% of institutional votes were cast against.
  • One independent joined. Vishal Gupta joined on 28 Oct 2024.
  • Executive seats were added. Mukulika Baid, a promoter-family non-executive director, stepped down on 6 May 2025, the day Vishal Baid became an executive director; Pankaj Kumar Gupta, the head of operations, followed on 8 Aug 2025.

The executive team below the board combines long-serving Polymed managers with hires made in 2024-26 for strategy, India and APAC, Brazil and renal, and the chief executives of the acquired companies.

How to read this report

Scope. This is an initiating-coverage report on the business and the industry. It has no earnings estimates, valuation, rating or target price. Where management has given guidance, it is reported as management's target and attributed to the call or presentation in which it was given.

Every number is traceable.

  • Each figure is drawn from a fact ledger built from company filings, presentations, call transcripts, rating-agency rationales, regulator texts and peer offer documents.
  • Hover over any number, or press on it on a touch screen, to see the source document, its date and the page or slide.
  • Figures computed by us (shares, growth rates, CAGRs, currency conversions) are labelled "our calculation", and the tooltip shows the formula and its inputs.
  • Market-research estimates from commercial vendors are labelled as such and used only as ranges.

Conventions.

  • Currency: rupee amounts are in Rs. mn and Rs. bn; company figures reported in crore or lakh are converted.
  • Periods: fiscal years end on 31 March (FY26 = April 2025 to March 2026) and quarters are written 1QFY27. European and other overseas subsidiaries report on calendar years (CY25).
  • Growth is year-on-year (yoy) unless stated.
  • Geography: "West Asia" refers to the region the company calls the Middle East.
  • "Standalone" is Poly Medicure Ltd, the Indian listed entity. "Consolidated" adds the subsidiaries and the equity-accounted associate.

What we do not know.

  • Presentations. They disclose revenue for five therapy lines: infusion, renal, cardiology, orthopaedics and "others".
  • The BRSR. The statutory Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report adds the share of standalone turnover for:
    • blood management and collection;
    • surgery and wound drainage;
    • urology;
    • anaesthesia and respiratory, in FY25;
    • prefilled flush syringes.

We convert these shares to rupees as our calculation.

  • Not disclosed. Diagnostics, gastroenterology and oncology are not broken out, and nothing is split at the consolidated level.
  • Our approach. We do not estimate splits beyond these disclosures. Where a line's size matters to the argument, we say it is not disclosed and list the question in the plant-visit question bank.
